speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day on Tuesday, December 6, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked for a statement as to reports on the dispatch of uranium from Canada to Soviet Russia. I can now answer that question.

Uranium
A search of the files of the Department of Munitions and Supply and the files of Eldorado Gold Mines Limited, the predecessor company of Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited, reveals the following facts:
On May 6, 1943, Eldorado Gold Mines Limited received an inquiry from their New York selling agent, Canadian Radium and Uranium Corporation, reporting an order from Chematar Incorporated, a firm of reputable New York exporters, for 500 pounds of black uranium oxide and 500 pounds of uranium nitrate. The inquiry reported that the destination of the material would be Soviet Russia, where it would be used for purposes connected with the prosecution of the war against nazi Germany; that the black uranium oxide would be used for ferro-uranium compounds, which in turn would be used in the production of armaments; and that the uranium nitrate would be used for medical purposes.
Eldorado Gold Mines Limited, which was then a privately-owned company, applied to the arms export permit branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce for a permit for the export of this material to the United States. This was granted by the zinc control branch of the metals controller on May 11, 1943, after it had been determined in the meantime that an export licence from the United States bureau of economic warfare had been issued.
The invoice of the material indicates that 500 pounds of black uranium oxide was billed at $1,275 and 500 pounds of uranium nitrate at $1,180, making a total billing of this material of $2,455.
The material was shipped on May 22, 1943, to Colonel A. N. Kotikov, resident representative of the Soviet government purchasing commission, air service depot of the air transport command, Gore Field, Great Falls, Montana, U.S.A. Payment for the shipment was deposited to the account of Eldorado Gold Mines at the Royal Bank of Canada, New York. The documents covering this shipment appear to be all in order.
Since its mining operations commenced, Eldorado had been producing uranium as a by-product of radium, which was the product of commercial interest at that time. Uranium was being sold for a number of uses through ordinary commercial channels. It was natural, therefore, that the order to which I have referred was treated as normal in both Canada and the United States of America.
At this time, 1943, only a very few persons -very few indeed-knew that experiments in the use of atomic energy for weapons purposes were proceeding. Those who did know, however, realized the wisdom of not calling
attention, by refusing to fill commercial orders, to uranium as a material suitable for any use other than the commercial uses to which it had been put for many years-uses such as those stated for the shipment in question.
It will also be remembered that in 1943 we were at the very height of the war against nazi Germany. Naturally it was then the policy of all the western allies to render any help possible to the Soviet union in the gigantic war struggle which that country was waging, with its allies, against the nazis.
I should add that, as atomic energy research developed, uranium became valuable, of course, for weapons purposes. In 1944, therefore, the Canadian government expropriated Eldorado Gold Mines Limited, in order to acquire closer control of this new strategic mineral.
After the acquisition of the property, Mr. Grant Glassco, of the firm of Clarkson, Gordon, Dilworth and Nash, was appointed by the government as a commissioner to examine into the affairs of Eldorado Gold Mines and the successor crown company, and was instructed particularly to look for irregularities in the shipment of radium and uranium.
Mr. Glassco's investigation revealed nothing to suggest that, in disposing of radioactive substances acquired by them, Eldorado and its agents dealt with customers other than the United States government and the ordinary buyers and users of these substances in Canada and the United States. A close check of the files shows no evidence of any shipment from Canada being re-exported other than the shipment I have just mentioned. .

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to ask the Postmaster General a number of general questions because he is new to the position and probably it would not be fair, but I should like to call his attention to certain conditions in the Toronto post office.

The revenue and surplus obtained by this department in Toronto is considerable. In
1946	it amounted to nearly $11 million, but then the cost of rural mail delivery was charged against the surplus revenue and in
1947	it dropped to a surplus of $8,773,000, and in 1948 to a surplus of $9,827,000.
In view of the large surplus, would it not be possible to pay something additional to the low-paid employees of the post office? Ten thousand extra employees will be taken on during the Christmas season to help deliver mail, and they should be paid at a proper rate. I can remember when the Minister of Public Works, along with the former postmaster general, Mr. Mulock, accompanied me on a tour of the Toronto terminal "A" post office in order to see the conditions under which the workers were sorting the mail. There is one large room there that is not really fit for human habitation.	There is hardly any ventilation.
Employees should not be asked to work under such intolerable conditions.
I should like to compare the postal revenue of Toronto with that of Montreal, the chairman's district. I admit that in Toronto considerable revenue is derived from the two large departmental stores, but, eliminating that factor, the postal receipts for Montreal are about $10,500,000 as compared with $16,500,000 for Toronto. Yet we have no post office in that city. There is a terminal "A" which was built by the old Grand Trunk and then taken over by the Canadian National Railways and used as the main post office.
I should like to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to the difficulty encountered when trying to buy postage stamps. Many people will be travelling this Christmas, and they should be able to buy stamps on the trains, or at least in the larger railway stations. Many soldiers will be going home for Christmas, and they should be able to let their people know that they are coming.
I should like to see some action taken to give the low-paid workers a better deal as to pay and working conditions. An effort should be made to improve their hours of labour and their working conditions. With the amount of second-class mail they have to handle, they all have humps on their backs. I have seen them delivering mail in the various districts of our city. The amount of second-class mail that must be delivered is an intolerable burden on the poor postman who has to go out in weather such as we are having at the present time. There should be some other way of making effective second-class delivery. I hope that the minister, if he gets an opportunity during

the recess, will come to Toronto and investigate the post office situation. He has a good deputy and other competent officials in the department. In fact I know of no department of the public service that has more support of the people than the post office.

at least one good holiday every few years in terms of weather and the facilities dependent thereupon.
Then there is the question of changing of classes. I understand that in some post offices the holidays are arranged on the basis of classes of employees. A difficult position arises where a man is promoted. I do not know what the grades are, but let us say that a mail porter is promoted to the position of clerk. It seems to me that his promotion would upset the particular rotation. I wonder how that is handled. Would he automatically go to the bottom of the list in his new position?
Perhaps the minister will comment on the questions I have raised.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
As to the question of holidays,
I presume the hon. member for Saskatoon is talking about annual leave. If that is the question, they must of necessity be spread over a period of time-actually over a period of nine months. The choice is made by seniority, senior members having a preference over others in the choice of the time of the year at which they wish to take their holidays.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Do they have such a preference every year?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Senior members, yes.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Every year?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is right; and it is done in accordance with the wish of the employees themselves. As to the second matter, the question is under review, in consultation with the employees.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I suggest that the wives and families of those at the bottom of the list on a seniority basis will hardly approve that regulation. I have heard there is some idea on the part of post office officials of changing the nine months' period to one of six months. I do not know whether there is a change of policy in view. The minister may be right when he says that the present system is the choice of the employees themselves, but I cannot conceive of such an arrangement being pleasant to most of them. Personally I do not think that rank or income should have any part in it. As a matter of fact those who enjoy higher incomes should be willing to give up these rights, because they can afford to maintain their wives and families at summer resorts, whereas the poorer employees cannot do so. There should be a system of rotation universally applied. When a senior employee has had his holidays in July, at a time when he can get the most enjoyment out of them, he should then go to the bottom of the list.

Supply-Post Office

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am informed that the system was organized as a result of the unanimous wish of the employees. The question has to do with consultations we are having with the employees at the present time, and if they wish a change to be made in this connection, the matter certainly will be studied. It does not follow that because a senior member has a priority of choice for his vacation period, he will of necessity choose July or August. He might be a hunter, a fisherman, or a ski enthusiast, and might very well choose times suitable for the enjoyment of such recreations to take his vacation.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I suggest that ninety-five per cent of the people living in our climate would choose the summer months if they had a choice in the matter. The minister suggested that this was done as a result of the wish of the employees themselves. Does he mean the employees generally across Canada, or the employees in a particular unit, for instance, Winnipeg, Regina or Saskatoon?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It was the unanimous wish of all employee associations, and they are Canada-wide in scope.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The word "unanimous" means one hundred per cent.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is right. Of course we do not know what discussions took place within the associations, but the end result is one hundred per cent representation to us by the associations.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Following what the hon. member for Saskatoon has said, I should like to say a word on this subject, because I think I know the issue involved. I have been associated with workers who regarded seniority as a very important matter. The hon. member for Saskatoon said he thought that ninety per cent of the employees might want a change made. I would agree with him if as individuals we were always able to look at things from the point of view of the majority. Unfortunately we are so constituted that generally we look at things from our own point of view. For years I was employed by an organization where seniority prevailed, and that seniority meant that some men worked on the day shift and others worked on the night shift. While a man was on the night shift he was always in favour of what we called the swing shift, but the moment he got on days he insisted that seniority should prevail. That is what happens here. The post office employees are organized; they have their associations, and there they determine how these things should be done. I would be reluctant to have the

post office authorities make arbitrary decisions in these matters. In my opinion the best thing to do is leave it with the employees.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: We have a new Postmaster General now, and often that means some changes are made. Has the Postmaster General given any further consideration to the extension of rural mail delivery?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: These rural mail routes are being extended every week, almost every day. Applications are received, they are studied by the department, and whenever possible they are granted.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I forgot to include one question in my remarks. In view of the revenues of the department, is there any hope of going back to the one-cent rate for drop letters for city delivery and the two-cent rate anywhere in the dominion?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am afraid the answer would be that there is very little chance.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I wanted to ask the minister a question in connection with rural routes. I understand there is a regulation under which there must be four mail boxes to the mile, and that regulation works great hardship in many country districts. On the one hand you may have fairly populous sections; then there will be other sections in which only a few people live, all covered by the one rural route, which means that the average will not be four boxes to the mile. It seems to me this is an obsolete regulation; it has been in force for a good many years, and I believe the time has come when people in the country districts should have daily mail delivery. In view of the large surplus the post office had last year, amounting to some $10 million, I do not see why this regulation should not be changed and the whole system revised.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask a question in reference to the post office in the village of Rothesay. I mentioned this matter last year. The situation there is almost intolerable. Rothesay is one of the finest villages in the maritime provinces, but it has a post office which would be a disgrace to any country crossroad. There are two large private schools at that point, a boys' school and a girls' school, in addition to a consolidated school; the population of that part of the county is growing rapidly, and I do hope the department will look into the matter. There have been a number of complaints, but nothing has been done as yet.
I would ask the minister to give the matter attention.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: As to the first question, increased costs have affected the Post Office Department just as much as they have affected other departments, and the various extensions of service that have been given have quickly diminished our surplus. It is not, as the hon. member said, a surplus of $10 million; it has been diminished to $2 million.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The surplus last year was $10 million.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Yes, but this year it is only $2 million. If we grant too many extensions we may very well find ourselves in the red next year. As to the second question, I shall study the case of the post office the hon. member has mentioned.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I have three questions to direct to the minister. As he will remember, I have had some correspondence with him in connection with the special stenographic allowance of $5 a month, which affects some 200 stenographers in the Post Office Department. On October 21 he advised me that he was going to discuss the matter with the civil service commission to see if something could be done.
The second question has to do with the carriage of mail by the ships of the C.N.R. around the coast of Newfoundland. I understand the present situation is that the mail is carried by crew members in their off-watch hours, in other words in their free time. Often a man will have to carry a bag of mail on his back for a mile or two, and I do not believe any provision has been made for compensation. Perhaps the minister could tell me whether the matter is being discussed, or what is the position.
The third question has to do with a comparatively minor matter, that is, the post office at Holyrood, as to which the minister will remember we had some correspondence. On November 11 I asked him for some information, but the matter probably slipped his mind. On November 8 he said he would inform me when an appointment was made, and since that time I have learned that an appointment was made on November 1. I was further informed that the appointment was made upon my recommendation, though certainly there was no recommendation of any kind made by me. I do not know how appointments in connection with these small post offices are made generally, but in our province they used to be more or less given to people who needed the little income obtained from operating the post office and supplying the service. In this case, however, I understand the appointment went to the
Supply-Post Office
wife of a wealthy merchant in the village of Holyrood, so I would certainly like to keep my skirts clear in that matter.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
As to the special stenographic compensation, that was disallowed or abolished, not only in the Post Office Department but in all departments, under an order in council passed September 21, 1949, effective October 1, 1949. We have made certain representations to the civil service commission in that regard, but up to the present there has been no change in that policy.
As to the second question, I may tell the hon. member that the matter is under active consideration and an answer will be forthcoming in due course.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Then may I say that compensation will be given these crew members?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I did not say that; I said we were considering the matter.
As to the third question, I am sorry I do not remember the circumstances in connection with the post office at Holyrood, but I shall have it checked and see what can be done.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister a question with respect to post office accommodation in two localities. I am well aware that the construction of new post office buildings comes under the Minister of Public Works, but I believe that post office accommodation generally is initiated through the Postmaster General. First I should like to ask about post office accommodation at Coleman, Alberta?
During the war years application was made for better post office accommodation. At that time the reason given for not providing such accommodation was that, because of the war, materials were scarce and perhaps skilled labour was unobtainable, and as a result the government were not carrying on any extensive construction. I believe that was a good reason. But within the last few weeks the application has been made again. Perhaps it is a little too soon to ask what progress has been made in that respect. I should be happy to follow up this discussion with documentary memoranda to the minister, but I know that he has been written to by the board of trade, and perhaps others. I understand the process is that application is made to the minister. Perhaps there are inspectors sent from the department, then recommendations are passed on to the Department of Public Works, and, from there on, something is either done or not done. Can the minister indicate what progress has been made in that respect?
While I am on my feet I wish to ask a second question; it is in respect to post office

Supply-Post Office
accommodation at Nanton, Alberta. I should like to know what progress is being made there. The minister may have seen a return that was brought down in the house about a month ago in regard to that matter. I am not going to elaborate on it. The return did not show a pleasant picture as to negotiations respecting accommodation over the past few years at Nanton. The final result, however, is that the present postmaster was told to furnish better accommodation. That was the understanding. Does the minister care to say what progress has been made in that regard?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The first question has to do with the post office at Coleman. The revenue of that office is $15,410 a year. At Nanton it is $9,300. I might tell the hon. member for Macleod that the situation about which he has just spoken is not restricted to those two places; it is general throughout the dominion. The department is greatly concerned about it, because it hampers our operations throughout Canada. There is a big backlog of construction to be undertaken. We have adopted the practice of recommending to the Department of Public Works the construction of buildings in places where the revenue is over $10,000. Among those offices a priority has been established in the public works department. We are pushing the construction of these post offices as much as we possibly can, because every building constructed will help us in our service. Beyond that I do not care to go.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I will say just a further word with respect to the post office at Coleman. The situation is serious. The building is not adequate; it is extremely old, and there are not enough post boxes. While the minister says that the Coleman office has a revenue of around $15,000, the population of Coleman is over 4,000. Application has been made. I will follow it up with a letter to the minister. I wish that he would give every possible consideration to Coleman. With respect to Nanton, I will not ask a question but I will urge the minister to see that the plans that are now ready are speeded up as much as possible.
I have a question on another matter. Will the minister inform the committee what the procedure is with respect to contracts or agreements for the printing of postage stamps? Does that come under the Post Office Department, or under the Department of Finance? I believe there are several engraving companies. What is the procedure? Are tenders asked for? On what basis are contracts let?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It comes under the Minister of Finance, but we are consulted as to the

printing of the stamps. The printing of postage stamps is provided for by contract. The duration of the current agreement with the manufacturer, the Canadian Bank Note Company, is from October 5, 1948 to March 31, 1950.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: For the printing of postage stamps they are carried over a period of time?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is right-under contract.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: How did they get the contract? Did they make a bid? Does the other company also make a bid?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Public tender.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I did not intend to question the minister about the construction of post offices, but as he himself has referred to the matter, there is a question I should like to ask him. In the public works estimates in the last session of the last parliament the Minister of Public Works had an estimate of $35,000 for a building in the town of Dominion, Nova Scotia, to replace an inadequate building. Replacement of this building has been promised over the last ten years, but nothing has been done. I understand that an official of the department looked over a building that might be purchased. I do not know how true this is, but I have been informed that local patronage skulduggery has prevented the spending of that $35,000 to improve the service there. Does the minister know anything about it?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
The revenue from the
Dominion office is $3,854. It is therefore not a project that the Post Office Department will recommend. The building he refers to is probably a public works project. If public works erects a building and offers us some space, of course we will take it, but it is not at the initiative of the Post Office Department that the building is being erected, if there is one being erected.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is quite right. The public works department did their part. They made the appropriation of $35,000 to build that post office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: And other things.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: If they are to build a post office, the building then belongs to the minister's department. It was to be built exclusively for the purpose of providing his department with adequate facilities in that particular town.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Was there to be only a post office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: In any event they would keep the title to the property. It does not pass to the Post Office Department.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I do not care who has the title. What I am concerned about is the performance of the service, and why that $35,000 has not been spent for the purpose for which it was intended.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member will have to ask the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I intend to do so.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: In the estimates this year for the town of Dominion there is a vote of $25,000 for a public building, not a post office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: He has cut it down $10,000. You fellows were slow. You should have got that money spent and had this post office building constructed. I had no intention of raising the question with the minister; but when I heard him answer questions asked by the hon. member for Macleod with regard to the construction of buildings, I thought I might as well find out what he knows about this particular case.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: How is it that the town of Dominion, in Cape Breton, with a revenue of only $4,000, can get a post office, and the village of Rothesay, with a revenue of twice that amount, cannot get one?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: As I have just said to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, it is not a post office building; it is a public building put up by public works, for some purpose of which I am not aware.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like many ather hon. members I regret that the Postmaster General did not make a statement. It would have saved a great deal of time when we are hurrying to get through his estimates. Had he made a statement he could have given us post office policy, but now we have to dig in and ask a hundred and one questions. However, in his wisdom he did not see fit to make a statement; therefore we shall have to extract from him, by the best means possible, the information we require.
One thing I did not know is that post office revenue had shrunk and that the net profit had dropped from $13 million to about $2 million. I cannot say that that is owing to a reduction in postage rates. A few years ago postal rates were raised 33J per cent. The letter rate was raised from three to four cents, and that increase is still with us. I would not urge that the rate be reduced 33J per cent and put back to where it was before if the money were used to give rural mail couriers a decent living wage.
Supply-Post Office
There are a number of things that I wish to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General. The first is what I understand to be the new policy of the department in calling for tenders in the rural mail districts. I do not know whether I am properly informed, but I understand that before a man can tender on a rural mail route he must have certain equipment-and some of it is expensive-to carry on the work. Is this so? Has the policy changed in that regard?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Has the hon. member any more questions?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Yes, twenty-five more.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is that the revenue of the post office has not shrunk as the hon. member for Queens has just asserted. What is true is that we have been giving better service, and that therefore our costs have increased in comparison with the revenue. Our costs having increased, of course our profit is less. We have absorbed the increased costs instead of asking for an increase in postal rates.
So far as rural mail is concerned, there is no new basis. It is true that in certain contracts a certain kind of equipment is required, but that is not new policy. It has always been that way, because we want to be sure that whoever gets the contract is equipped to carry it out.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Either the minister is right or I am right, or we are both wrong. I hold in my hand a copy of a mail contract which reads: "Sealed tenders will be addressed . . ." and so on . . . "to the Postmaster General." It goes on and gives a list of the mileage, where to call, and so on. Then there is this vital part: "Any tenders submitted must be with the clear understanding that this service is to be performed by a truck in summer and a snowmobile in the wintertime." That is certainly new policy.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What is the service to which the hon. member is referring?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Rural mail route No. 3, in Queens county, a distance of twenty-one miles. Just imagine asking a man, before he can expect to get a contract, to provide himself with a truck and a snowmobile! It is not possible to buy these vehicles at less than $4,500 or $4,000. The department is asking a man to provide himself with equipment at a cost of $4,000 to tender for a job on which he can get only $1,000 a year for four years, and then he would have to tender over again. It seems to me to be a ridiculous policy. If that is to be the policy, the department will have to provide the mail couriers with this equipment and charge them a rental. How

Supply-Post Office
can you expect a mail courier to pay $4,500 for equipment to run a service out of which he gets only $1,000 a year for four years? There is no guarantee of anything. That is driving the rural mail couriers to a pretty hard decision if they are to tender.
There is another thing with reference to tendering that I think is a new policy, and it is this. Suppose a man has had a contract- and I can give the names of a couple of men who have had contracts for from ten years to thirty years and have given the best of service. No civil servants in any part of Canada could give better service than the service that these men have given, and I can mention their names. They have worked all through the years at a salary or indemnity which was not giving them a livelihood. Now they are getting a little older, and what happens? When they ask for a little more for the mail route-and I do not believe anybody else would tender against them-the department says that it is too high in comparison with other mail routes. That is not much of an argument when some of the other mail routes are not paying a living wage. The question then arises, what is the man to do? Instead of the department making some compromise with him, as I think it should do, and give him a chance, it scouts around and finds some veteran who is getting a small pension of $300 or $400 a year, and says to him: You can tender at $300 or $400 less than the regular contract man. I have no objection to veterans getting the contracts, but I do object to a veteran having to use his small pension to tender in opposition to the other man. The Postmaster General should clear up that matter.
1 should now like to refer to our own post office in Charlottetown. Prince Edward Island was the ninth province. Now there are ten. It is an island province, and it is entitled to whatever consideration is given to the other provinces of Canada in the way of transportation, postal accommodation or anything else. We are not rated as a province at all.
Under the new set-up the department has put in a regional controller, and that is all right. This regional controller is situated at Moncton. But under the regional controller there is a district director of postal services. One of these is located at Saint John and the other at Halifax. We should have a district director in Charlottetown, where we have a good post office staff. But no; we are attached to New Brunswick. I do not know what Newfoundland is going to be attached to, whether it will be with Nova Scotia or will have its own district director of postal services.

I should like to know why our province is not treated properly in this regard. Prince Edward Island should have a district director of postal services. Of late years under this government we have become accustomed to that type of treatment. A year ago it took away from our city the branch of the Bank of Canada. However, we have forced them to the point where they are going to put it back. The government has also placed the headquarters of the Bank of Canada, as it affects Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick. It has also taken away from us the head of the fruits and vegetables branch, and placed that centre in Saint John, New Brunswick.
I say we should not stand for it any longer. We should be told whether we are to have a district director of postal services in Prince Edward Island, to which we are entitled. Any important postal business in our province must pass through the Charlottetown post office, then to the district director, and then on to the regional controller at Moncton. From there it goes to Ottawa before any decision can be made in any matter of vital importance in connection with our postal service. I hope the Postmaster General will look carefully into this matter with a view to giving us better treatment.
The attention of the Postmaster General has been called to the fact that in the post office at Charlottetown there is a position known as the vendor of postage stamps. It is one worthy of some consideration, especially at the present time. The man who has been in charge of the office for the last forty-nine years, Mr. Aubrey F. Brown, has been one of the best public servants to be found anywhere. He accepted his position under contract on November 13 forty-nine years ago. He is now in his fiftieth year of service. His contract was for the sale of postage stamps, cards and the like, and was made under an agreement with the government of that day.
This man has continued his work without one complaint. His hours are long; I do not know why the authorities have made him work such long hours. Under his contract he must go to work at eight o'clock in the morning and must keep his office open until eight o'clock in the evening, with no time for lunch or dinner. If he leaves for any length of time, or is ill, he must employ and pay for assistance. This is certainly contrary to all the labour laws of this or any other country. He has three days' holidays throughout the year. It would seem that the postal department are endeavouring to get rid of him and to handle postage stamps through the main office, at

which point they will have to hire two clerks to do the same work. This will give employment to two people and throw one out of employment.
The procedure of getting rid of this man seems peculiar. His contract calls for two per cent on all sales of postage stamps, cards and the like in that postal area. A few years ago when he applied for a higher rate he was told that he could not have it, because the contract called for only two per cent on all sales. At this time, however, the postal department are putting in meter machines. It may be said that for the businessman these machines are more efficient, but when this man suggested that he should receive his two per cent on the amount handled by the machine, which has reduced his income by over fifty per cent, he was ;old he could not have it. The postal department take all the revenue and do not allow aim the two per cent to which his contract, signed by the postal department, entitles him.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is not a contract.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It was a contract when it was drawn, but it has never been renewed. The contract is broken when they want to [DOT]elieve him of his job. The desire seems to )e to put in two clerks to do the work he has leen doing for so long without complaint. \fter all those years of service, in view )f the small wages he was able to make-and t was all on a commission basis of two per sent, with some lean years-he is just able
0	make a living. He has always had to smploy an assistant for an hour at noon and in hour and a half in the evening, and this las taken a considerable portion of his evenue. I hope that some arrangement can >e made by which he can be retired on a small >ension. It may be said that he is not a sivil servant. But there is still no reason vhy the government should not make some illowance for his service of fifty years. I vould ask the Postmaster General and his issistants to take this into consideration so bat some satisfactory settlement may be made.
There are other matters I shall discuss later, iut with one of them I will deal now. It vas suggested to the postmaster general vho held office three years ago that a com-nittee be set up to study rural mail problems, 'he Postmaster General's reply to that, as eported on page 360 of Hansard of February 2, 1947, was as follows:
1	have no objection to having a committee con-ider this matter in an effort to improve the service.
Supply-Post Office
In the following year, in reply to a question asked by myself, the minister stated, as reported on page 1039 of Hansard of February 10, 1948:
It is not the intention of the government to establish a committee, but as I said before, a bill will be brought in to give authority to make further supplementary payments.
The Postmaster General might indicate whether at the next session he will set up a committee to study the problem of the rural mail courier. It is a problem that needs consideration.
The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the reduction of $5 a month in stenographers' salaries. According to the Postmaster General that reduction took place right across Canada. I should like to know if the government authorized it.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Replying to the question relating to rural route No. 3, Queens county, and the matter of necessary equipment, the department does not establish what equipment is required; that is left to the inspector to determine. The department insists that service shall be given under all circumstances, that the mail must be delivered every day. At times the contract requires that snowmobiles be part of the equipment available so that the mail may be delivered without delay.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Has the department one contract containing a condition of that kind?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
There are quite a number of contracts in which the notices for tenders required that snowmobiles be provided. It might be that when a man makes his tender he has not a snowmobile, and I can quite understand that he would not purchase one before actually getting a contract. But no one has been prevented from getting a contract provided he can satisfy the department that he can acquire a snowmobile as part of the necessary equipment.
As to the men who have had contracts for ten and thirty years, I am sorry I have not the names. If the hon. member will supply me with the names, I shall have the matter investigated. I might say that as far as contracts are concerned, veterans have no priority. Also the amount of tender is not disclosed.
A complaint is made by the hon. member that there is no director located at Charlottetown. Directors are not appointed for each provincial district. We try to see that the directors are kept busy, and as the director in that part of the country would not have sufficient work from just one province, he is given jurisdiction over more than the one

Supply-Post Office
province. It is said that the post office inspector at Charlottetown must go to the director, then to another man and then to Ottawa, but that is not so. The post office inspector at Charlottetown has authority to deal directly with the department if he wishes to do so.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What is the need of having a director?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
We have to be kept informed in a general way of what is being done.
With regard to the stamp vendor, Mr. Brown has been a vendor of stamps for the last forty-nine years under a contract. He is not an employee of the government, and therefore we do not regulate the hours he keeps. His contract calls for certain things, and he is the one who is the employer.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Who signed the contract?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It was signed forty-nine years ago. I have not seen it.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Whom was it between?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I have not seen the contract. I do not know.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It is the general contract.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Is it a contract between the Post Office Department and the vendor?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am informed that actually there is no contract, that he is just allowed to continue as is.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I beg leave to say that there is a contract. There was a contract when he got the position, and the Post Office Department must have it somewhere in its archives.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I am informed that there was a contract, but it has not been renewed, that he is allowed to continue as is. Complaint is made about the remuneration he receives, but there would have to be a change in the legislation to correct that situation. Section 7, paragraph (o) of the Post Office Act reads:
. . . (o) grant licences to agents other than postmasters, for the sale to the public of postage stamps and stamped envelopes, and allow to such agents a commission not exceeding two per centum of the amount of their sales.
The vending machine to which the hon. member refers was put in to take care of the Christmas rush, and will be taken out in January. As this man is under contract, I do not think the question of pension can be considered for a minute. He is not an employee of the government, and I do not think a pension scheme could be evolved in that connection.
With regard to the reduction in stenographic pay, I have just drawn the attention of the hon. member to order in council 19/4847,

passed on September 21, 1949, to be effective October 1. I think about 200 of a total staff in the Post Office Department of about 42,000 were affected.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I was under the impression from a letter I received that the civil service commission had ordered this reduction.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The civil service commission recommended it.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It is now established that the government made the reduction. The minister says that according to law they can pay this stamp vendor only two per cent, but I would ask him to note that he is taking away from him fifty per cent of his revenue by the use of the meter machine. Not only is that so in the post office; the larger firms are being induced to put them in. This stamp vendor is entitled to two per cent on the sales indicated by the meter machine.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The authority given to the Postmaster General is to issue a licence. It is not an exclusive licence; it is a licence for the sale of postage stamps to the public.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: He had that licence under his contract.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
There is one question I should like to ask the minister about rural mai] boxes. As I understand it, at the present time they are purchased by the department from one source and are sold to or put at the disposal of persons on rural mail routes. 1 am also informed that the department does not permit persons on rural mail routes tc have other mail boxes, or to purchase boxes from other sources, even though other boxes may comply in all respects with the specifications followed in the case of boxes furnished by the department. I should like to ask the minister whether this monopolistic arrangement prevails, and, if so, why persons on rura: mail routes should not be at liberty tc purchase boxes for their own use from any source they choose, provided that they comply with the specifications that apply to boxes furnished through the department.
I am told that this rigidity on the par of the department prevents people from having anything more ornamental in the way of a mail box, and that highway authorities in Ontario, in the case of some of the nev improved highways, have felt that the boxes in use, furnished by the department, are no very ornamental. May I ask the minister foi a statement on this matter?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglintor has given only one side of the case; we mus also look at the other side. People could pu up all sorts of makeshift boxes.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I expressly said that whateve: is done must, of course, comply with thi

specifications of the department in relation to the box. All I am saying is that when anyone is prepared to comply with the specifications of the department in the case of his own box, there should not be any requirement that the boxes must all come from one particular source.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am informed that the complaints about the boxes really resolved themselves into suggestions regarding the supports. Certain gentlemen visited the office yesterday, and an arrangement is being worked out so that it will be taken care of.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Am I to conclude then, that so far as the department is concerned there is nothing to prevent someone else from supplying mail boxes to persons on rural routes, provided that they comply with the specifications laid down by the department as to the type of mail box that is now in use?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: We cannot possibly do that. There must be uniformity in the boxes throughout, and if we allow an exception in one direction we will have to authorize it in the other direction. We want our boxes to be uniform, and not makeshift. One way or the other it is the same thing.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Does that mean the boxes must all be purchased from the same source?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The answer is yes.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
That is a monopolistic
arrangement.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The post office is probably the biggest monopoly in Canada.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: If that is so, in my own district I have seen about half a dozen different sizes and types of boxes that have been provided by the department.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: In different years.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: There is nothing uniform about them at all.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: We are not going to ask people to change their boxes every time there is a change in the type. At the present time we have a new type of box which I believe will hold twice as much as the old one. We are not going to force all the users of boxes to change the ones they have already purchased.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Following the question about a monopoly in the making of the boxes by one particular firm, will the Postmaster General tell the committee whether the price that the resident pays for the box is also stipulated?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
The answer is yes. There is no monopoly, because it is under contract,
45781-185J
Supply-Post Office
and before the contract is let, tenders are called for. The contract awarded is to the lowest tenderer.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What is the normal price charged for these boxes?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Four dollars.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Would that price compete with anything people could make themselves?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: If a person made one box I imagine it would cost much more than the department would pay per box for the manufacture of thousands.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: This is the time of year when a good many people are sending food parcels overseas, chiefly to Great Britain. I am well aware there is a special rate on such parcels. In the first place, I should like to ask what the difference is between the rates applying to recognized Christmas food parcels and that applying to ordinary parcels?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The rates are as follows: Up to and including five pounds, 50 cents; up to and including ten pounds, $1; up to and including fifteen pounds, $1.50; up to and including twenty pounds, $2.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: My question concerned a comparison.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It is fifty cents less than the regular rate.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps that will help to console the man in the street, but sometimes he does not realize he is getting a special rate on these parcels. The point to which I want to draw the Postmaster General's attention is that the rates for such food parcels are set in five-pound divisions. For instance, I mailed a package the other day which I estimated to weigh about five pounds. Unfortunately it was five pounds five ounces, and therefore I had to pay the ten-pound rate for what was virtually a five-pound parcel. As I say, the man in the street does not appreciate that, and perhaps does not appreciate he is getting a cheaper rate on that particular type of parcel.
Is the five-pound idea merely a convenient figure to divide or multiply by? Was it chosen for that reason, or is there another reason why five-pound divisions were selected? I would not mind so much paying a rate for six pounds on a five pounds-five ounces parcel, but it seems to me it is too. much to pay double for a small parcel. Could the divisions not be in single pounds rather than five pounds? If one has a parcel that is an ounce or two over fifteen pounds, he pays the twenty-pound rate. Possibly the cheaper rate justifies that, and possibly not; but the people who are sending these parcels

Supply-Post Office
would much rather put the money expended on postage for the extra five pounds into additional food than give it to the department for not doing any work.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: These rates have been fixed in agreement with the British authorities. As to fixing another limit for the packages, let us take six pounds; the same thing will still happen if somebody has a package weighing six pounds one ounce. We will be in the same position. We have to fix a certain poundage and not go beyond it, because there would be no use in setting a limit of five pounds if we were to accept five and a half pounds or even five pounds one ounce. We have to fix a limit, and that limit has been set at five pounds, ten pounds, fifteen pounds and twenty pounds.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I was wondering why it had been fixed at five. Why not four, or six, or three?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That is the arrangement we have with Britain.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: My own suggestion is that one pound would cover it.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: An examination of the Post Office Department balance sheet indicates that in the past year it repeated its performance of previous years-that is, it piled up a considerable profit. In considering these profits we cannot be unmindful of the fact that the public works department bears a substantial burden so far as capital costs are concerned. The minister has not occupied his present office for very long, but I am sure that, like those who have preceded him as Postmaster General, he will be anxious to do everything possible to endear himself to the Canadian people. If he wishes to accomplish that purpose I suggest that a most effective way of doing so would be to recommend to the Minister of Finance, before the next session of parliament, that the four-cent postage rate be reduced by one cent. After all, that rate was increased during the war, and the minister might advise the Minister of Finance that the war has been over for some years. I am quite sure that if before the next session of parliament comes around the regular postage rate is reduced from four cents to three cents, it will meet with the general approval of the people.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I want to ask the Postmaster General one or two questions in connection with alterations to public buildings in which post offices are located, referring particularly to a public building in my own constituency. Has the Post Office Department any planning experts who advise the Department of Public Works when these alterations are being made?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The department has an engineer, but unfortunately he also is very hard pressed at the present time.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I ask that question because in the town of Dundas the government is spending between $30,000 and $40,000 on alterations to the public building in order to meet the needs of the Post Office Department. That is a two or three storey building, the second floor of which has been occupied for the past several years by the Veterans Land Act administration for that district. Now the post office needs more space, and that is why the alterations are being made. In the meantime I find that the Veterans Land Act administration is moving to Hamilton, and that the building in Dundas will revert to the condition it has been in for the last twenty-five years-that is, only half used.
There are several matters in connection with these alterations that I could mention, but the point is that the only steps necessary to make that additional space available to the post office would have been the installation of an elevator. Then the second floor of that building would have given all the space needed, and the people of Canada would have been saved more than $30,000. This is one project I feel was not fully considered, and in connection with which the planning was not properly done. Even after these alterations are carried out, the premises will be very unhandy from the point of view of the staff, and it seems to me if the postmaster had been consulted he could have offered suggestions which would have made these alterations much more satisfactory from the standpoint of both the staff and the public.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I shall bring that matter to the attention of our engineer and of my colleague the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What population must a town have before postal delivery service can be inaugurated?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It is not a question of the population of a city; it is a question of how many people are to be served. Two thousand points of call are usually required, provided that conditions for delivery are satisfactory and other requirements are met.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Then it is not on a population basis?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: No, it is not; it is the points of call.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
We are now considering item No. 307, dealing with departmental costs and so on. I want to put on record in a few words a request on behalf of a community in the eastern part of Toronto which is not serviced by a post office as such,

but where the department is renting suboffices. In that fast growing section, which now has a population of about 200,000, we require adequate postal facilities. I do not expect the minister to give me a reply now, but I am asking the department to give that community the same consideration that was given west Toronto, where a public building was established on Keele street. I am not asking for this just because west Toronto was given that consideration, but because these facilities are needed in east Toronto.
I am asking the departmental officials if they will make a study of the situation in that community, which in the last quarter of a century has increased in population from 10,000 or 15,000 to well over 200,000, and to get together with the Minister of Public Works to see if those people cannot be given a dominion public building to provide accommodation for the Post Office Department and other departments of government such as customs, excise, immigration and so on. At the present time if an individual or business firm wants to clear post office parcels or to bring anything through customs, it is necessary to go almost ten miles down into the busy heart of the city of Toronto, clogging traffic and taking all day to do a chore which might be done in an hour if the facilities were available in that community. In the last two years we have had more than a hundred new factories in the area of which I speak, and about which the officials will know; and it is developing rapidly for the reason that industries have no other place to go; they must come to the eastern section of the city.
Without a long petition, which I could easily obtain, without bombarding the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works with letters, I am making this request. All that is necessary, I think, is that a little common sense, good judgment and co-operation be shown by the officials of these two departments to see that this community, which is a city in itself, gets the facilities necessary if it is to conduct its business in a proper way.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: As usual we shall use our best judgment.

Item agreed to.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
308. Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices, $37,804,896.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
There is a matter that I was going to bring up on the first item,
Supply-Post Office
but the minister told me that this was the proper one. I understand that the department has adopted a new system with regard to letter carriers in the matter of their transportation when engaged in the delivery of mail. My understanding is that formerly letter carriers travelled free on streetcars, or at least that they did not have to pay fare while in uniform. They are now required to pay fare when they travel on streetcars in the course of the performance of their duties.
I should like to point out that the letter carrier is not in the position of an ordinary passenger. In the first place, he has his load of mail. He may have to use the streetcar several times a day in the course of his work. I was a streetcar conductor for many years, and I know that under those circumstances letter carriers had their transportation taken care of. I should like to have the assurance of the Postmaster General that this matter, whether it has been decided or not, will be reconsidered. At this time of the year when a person is expecting a Christmas box but receives one in reverse, it is not cricket, as the English would say. It may seem a small thing to us, but I assure the minister that it is not a small thing to the letter carrier. I should like to have the assurance of the Postmaster General that he will reconsider the matter.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
For some time the letter
carriers have been getting free transportation while in uniform. The contracts were to the effect that the letter carriers would be allowed transportation from the post office to the beginning of their routes and from the end of their routes back to the post office. It never was the intention to include in those contracts travel between their places of residence and the post office. There is no special reason why they should be given a privilege which is not enjoyed by other employees who have to pay their fare from their homes to work and from work to their homes.
At the present time we are considering the various contracts relating to city transportation. In Ottawa we inaugurated a system of tickets. We are looking at the rates in the various other cities, because we are now faced with a demand by the transportation companies for increases in the current amounts of the contracts. In Montreal, for instance, the demand is for an increase of 33J per cent. We are considering those contracts at the present time. We have not yet made any final decision.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I wonder whether I understood the Postmaster General aright. Instead of travelling free when in uniform, the letter

Supply-Post Office
carriers now get tickets that will take them from their homes to the post office and from the post office to their homes?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: No. They have no ticket when travelling from their homes to the post office, but they are entitled to a ticket from the post office to the beginning of their routes or from the end of their routes back to the post office, or back to their homes if the distance between the end of their routes and their homes is greater by at least five hundred yards than the distance from their home to the post office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Can the
minister give us a progress report as to what is happening to the suggested new post office in Winnipeg?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am told that the plans are in process of being completed by our department, and should be turned over to the public works department in a matter of days.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Have there been any complaints from the owners of properties that were expropriated? Have all the dealings been on an amicable basis, or have there been complaints?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: To our knowledge there have been no complaints.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: It is a well-known fact that if a man serves in the House of Commons for fifteen, twenty, twenty-five or thirty years and then does not wish to go to the Senate, or does not have an opportunity to do so, when he is no longer a member of the house he is out of all the things that went to make him an efficient member. A corporation will give a pension. Civil servants get a pension. But a member of parliament will get nothing but bumps. I suggest to the Postmaster General that if a man serves twenty-five or more years in the house he should at least have his franking privilege, whether he is a former private member or former prime minister. I would ask the Postmaster General to consider this request. I think the member of parliament has earned it. I do not doubt that some of these men today get letters with no stamps on them, and are obliged to pay double postage.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: While we are on this item, can the minister tell me just what constitutes need for a post office in a district?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What does the hon. member mean by "need"?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: How badly does a district or a municipality have to be in need of a post office before it gets one? I am thinking now of a postal station, not just a sub-office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean a post office building?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The Post Office Department of course considers the needs of the various municipalities concerned. It is concerned also with the size of the municipality, and the revenue. Where the post office has a revenue of less than $3,000, it is up to the postmaster himself to supply the necessary premises. With regard to post offices with revenue of $3,000 up to $10,000, it is the public works department which usually arranges for locations, by way of lease, after conferring with our officials as to suitability of location. With regard to offices with more than $10,000 revenue, it is the principle of the department that post office buildings should be built, and recommendations to that effect are made to the public works department. As I explained this morning, there is a big backlog in this respect, owing to scarcity of materials, etc. We have had to establish some sort of priority with regard to these. We are pushing the public works department to erect these buildings, because we realize that in order to give good service we must have good buildings.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Is it the officials of the Post Office Department who determine whether there is a genuine need for a post office building?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The inspector usually makes the report.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I have been asked by some of the members from Quebec and Ontario to raise a question with regard to franking. It has no particular application to the members who live a considerable distance from Ottawa, but rather to members from Ontario and Quebec who are frequently in the city on government business and have communications to send from the parliament buildings. I understand that the franking privilege ends ten days after the session ends. Some of these members request that the franking privilege be extended so that when they are in Ottawa on business they may frank their letters from the buildings here. I appreciate the fact that there might be an abuse of the privilege, but I am asking that the minister give the matter his consideration.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
The suggestion certainly has merit, but we would have to amend the act. Section 43 of the act respecting postal service, in dealing with the frank, says:
. . . letters and other mailable matter addressed to or by any member of either house at the seat of government, during any session of parliament, or to any of the members at the seat of government as aforesaid, during the ten days next before the meeting of parliament, shall be free of Canada postage.

Therefore the law itself would have to be amended.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I should like to refer to a request for a post office in my constituency. The former postmaster general promised to give it priority. A contract was called for this post office in 1939. The contract was let, but on account of the war construction was stopped. A piece of land was secured in 1939. When the contract was stopped the people in that district were promised that as soon as the war ended a post office would be erected. At that time the revenue was some $3,593. Today the revenue is beyond $9,000. The place is Plaster Rock, New Brunswick, a large lumbering and agricultural centre. In 1939 they had a large building. Today they have moved out of that building into a small building. The postmaster has only a small building in which to work. It is not becoming to the town. Since the revenues of this office have increased I hope that it will receive attention soon.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I shall be pleased to look into the matter.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I have not very much to say except commendation of the Post Office Department. So far as the public are concerned in my constituency they have been getting, on the whole, good service. The matter of how many boxes to the mile entitle a community to a rural mail service was brought up this morning. In my constituency there is one locality that had a rural route in previous years. The operation for over a mile in that district was discontinued. Justification for its discontinuance, as explained to me, was that instead of having four boxholders it had only three to the mile. I think it is desirable that the three boxholders should be served. Those who have been boxholders in the past should not be denied the privilege of a rural mail delivery.
Today we are at some disadvantage in discussing these estimates because we have not the last report from the department. I was able to get only the annual report for the year ended March 31, 1948, which is a year and nine months ago. Why should we not have the report for the year ending March 31, 1949?
The minister has stated the conditions under which post office buildings are erected. There is one locality in my constituency, namely, Pugwash, a seaboard town, the annual revenue of which must be practically up to the $10,000 minimum requirement. In
Supply-Post Office
any event, that community should be provided with a post office building. The building they have is not adequate to serve the requirements. I am sure there are many communities that have post office buildings where the revenue is much less than in the town of Pugwash.
Our service has been kept fairly free of political influence. I have had few complaints. That is a good thing for the service and a good thing for the department, and the public appreciate it. Where we do get complaints of political interference with the service and with appointments it has a bad effect all round. I believe it should be the policy of the department to keep it free from such influence. I have brought one instance to the attention of the minister. I shall not refer to it here. If the circumstances are as represented to me the department should take steps to correct this interference.
One of the complaints I have had in my constituency in recent years is the unfairness of the department in granting bonuses. Some mail couriers who made application for bonuses and pressed their claims were granted these bonuses or subsidies. Other couriers who felt that it was their duty to carry out their contracts, in accordance with the terms under which they tendered, did not know that increases were being paid and did not press for additional allowances. They continued to carry out their contracts at very small remuneration, while others received these bonuses. I consider that very unfair. Every person carrying on a service under the same conditions should have an equal chance to get these additional amounts which were granted during the war. I do not believe these bonuses are being renewed at the present time. That is one of the serious complaints I have had in my constituency. The department has shown great unfairness and discrimination to persdns who got these increases.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The authority for the bonus was abolished on March 31, 1949. I thank the hon. member for his suggestion as to the reduction in the number of people holding boxes per mile. We are always eager to improve the service and we shall certainly study his suggestion. I accept with pleasure and thanks the hon. member's praise.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to a petition, which I received in August before I left St. John's, from two small settlements near a post office in Trepassey. The two places are Daniel's Point and Small Point. When I received those petitions I got in touch with the district inspector, and he told me I would hear about

Supply-Post Office
it when I got to Ottawa. Well, I have been here three months and I have not heard anything about it. I wrote to the Postmaster General a day or so ago. I wonder whether he is in a position to tell me if it has been decided or not.
In support of the request I may say that between 1931 and 1933 we had a depression in Newfoundland also, and we cut out a lot of post offices, cut down the service greatly. Now times are better and business is better, and there is a lot more mail coming. These two settlements are from four to six miles in from the main post office, and the practice is to send children across in dories to the post office. If they have to walk, they must go a distance of five or six miles each way to bring the mail back.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I have not seen the letter to which the hon. member refers. I shall certainly give it my best attention.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
1 put in a
petition.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The hon. member referred to a letter sent to me, which I have not yet seen.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Just a couple of days ago.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I have not seen it yet.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Why have we not the report of this department for the past year? It is about twenty-one months since the last report.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am informed this is due to delay in printing, which is brought about by the heavy business of the session.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The committee should have in its hands a report as important as this one before we have to deal with the estimates of the Post Office Department or any other department. It is most unfair to the members.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: And to the minister, too. He has not got it either.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Have any of the minister's officials looked into the need for a post office in Forest Hill and York township? A request was sent to the postal authorities about three years ago, at which time we were informed of the shortage of materials. That request has been renewed by some of the councils. There is a community of around 100,000 people. The post office nearest to some of these people is at least seven or eight miles away. I am informed that there is difficulty in mailing parcels or securing money orders for people outside Canada. In most instances the residents have to go to the postal station for that service.
(Mr. Browne (St. John's West).]
I have received a good deal of criticism concerning some of the substations tucked away in little corners of drugstores and grocery stores. I have been in some where a person who goes for mail is the last person to receive attention. Those who are making purchases are served first. I wonder if any of the departmental officials have looked into that situation in York township and Forest Hill?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: A delegation was received recently and we are now studying their recommendations.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The minister has said there are 25,000 temporary employees taken on for the Christmas rush. The estimates disclose an expenditure of almost $10,250,000 for temporary assistance. How many of those temporary employees are on a full yearly basis?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: In this department on March 31, 1949, the number was 4,535 temporary employees on a yearly basis.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Why are so many of these temporary employees kept on so long on a temporary basis?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am informed the chief reasons are, first, the question of the quota per post office and, secondly, that certain people are not yet qualified through examination of the civil service. There are also other people acting as replacements for those on vacation, and matters of that kind. The two first named reasons are the chief ones.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
May I impress upon the Postmaster General the claim for a postal station in the Weston and Brooklands area of Winnipeg. I have had correspondence with him concerning this proposal, and would refer particularly to his letter to me of October 19. The information contained in that letter, bearing in mind what he said a few moments ago, strengthens my plea for consideration of this proposal.
