speechtext:
['I had intended to make a statement on the next item, but in view of the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary West it might be advisable to make it at this time.
The committee will recall the statement I made the other evening with respect to cortisone and ACTH, and the circumstances surrounding them, which I felt could be made public at that time. In view of certain conferences which have since taken place here in Ottawa and elsewhere, it is now possible to supplement that statement.
On November 28 I announced that limited supplies of cortisone manufactured in the United States would be made available after January 1 by Merck and Company Limited, Montreal, for research to be undertaken in Canada. Today I can reveal that, as a result of negotiations that have been going on for some time, Connaught Medical Research Laboratories at the university of Toronto are going to undertake immediately to get production of ACTH under way in Canada for investigation and clinical research by Canadian scientists.
The federal government, the Canadian packing industry and the university of Toronto are all co-operating in the project of producing ACTH in Canada. Supplies of ACTH made available in this country will be allocated exclusively for research by a special committee of eminent Canadian medical men named by the president of the national research council. This committee, besides advising on the allocation of ACTH, will approve financial support for research on both ACTH and cortisone to ensure that all available facilities in Canada are fully utilized to speed the research program. The cost, estimated at about three-quarters of a million dollars in the first instance, will be provided for by the federal government through the national health grants and the national research council.
ACTH, like cortisone, seems to hold promise for the treatment of a number of diseases, but since on the basis of present knowledge only exceedingly small quantities of these drugs can be produced, they will be used exclusively for research to determine their

full effects, to discover new or improved methods of production, and to study the possibility of developing related products having similar efEects. Only by limiting these drugs strictly for research purposes now can we hope for progress in finding out how to produce enough for whatever treatment purposes are proved to be of lasting value.
The medical scientists with whom there has been collaboration have urged that persons suffering from arthritis or other disease for which ACTH and cortisone are possible remedies should not neglect the treatment they may presently be taking. As I mentioned in the house a few days ago, with Dr. Cameron, deputy minister of National Health and Welfare, I had an opportunity in New York recently of discussing these drugs with Drs. Hench and Kendall of the Mayo clinic, who are best known among the many scientists who have been associated with their development and use. Both emphasized to us that no responsible prediction could be given as to when adequate quantities of cortisone will be available for treatment purposes. Canadian medical scientists have urged me to state that the same is true for ACTH.
ACTH-known to scientists as the adreno-corticotrophic hormone-is a substance obtained from the tiny pituitary gland located in the centre of the brain of animals. It gives promise of highly important discoveries which may lead to advances in the treatment of a number of diseases. It is, for example, believed to stimulate the body to produce its own cortisone, which has already been found by Drs. Kendall and Hench of the Mayo clinic to produce "encouraging results" in the treatment of certain types of arthritis.
Up to the present, ACTH is being extracted from the pituitary glands of hogs. This gland is about the size of a pea and only a fraction of it contains the hormone. It is estimated that 1,700 hogs produce a pound of glands, and that 400,000 hogs are needed to yield a pound of ACTH.
At present, the entire production of ACTH in the United States is 60 pounds per year, enough for the continuous treatment of only a thousand patients. ACTH can also be obtained from the glands of cattle and sheep, but the yield is not nearly as large as from hogs.
What I am going to say now is said in part with the view of placing on the record the contribution made in this highly important field by our own Canadian scientists-medical men and chemists, particularly steroid chemists.
Since the interest and help of the Canadian packing industry is assured, the maximum
Supply-National Health and Welfare amount of glands will be collected. This entails special arrangements being made, as the glands must be quickly removed from the slaughtered animal, frozen and kept frozen until processed. Dr. R. D. Defries, the director of the Connaught Medical Research Laboratories, is my authority for saying that during the past few months Armour Laboratories in Chicago have been able to forward limited supplies of ACTH to a few centres in Canada for investigation. Although chemists in Canadian laboratories have been interested in this material for some time there has as yet been no production trere of this drug in more than the most minute experimental quantities.
To ensure a continuing supply of ACTH in this country without drawing heavily upon the necessarily restricted supply available for research in the United States, it is planned to use as large a quantity as possible of pituitary glands from Canadian sources. Small quantities will be used at first to develop a method of production in the Connaught Laboratories and the balance will be forwarded to Armour Laboratories in Chicago, who have developed successful processing techniques and will make a supply of ACTH available for use in this country. I am further empowered to state that as soon as production is well established, in keeping with the general policy of this widely known research organization, the product will be made available at the minimum cost.
To assist in financing this undertaking, with the co-operation of the Ontario department of health, a federal grant has been approved from the funds available for public health research under the national health program. An equal amount is being granted by the medical division of the national research council. These grants will be used for developing the process of production.
In the initial stage of making ACTH and cortisone available for research in Canada, an expenditure of as much as three quarters of a million dollars will probably be required during the first year. It is not possible yet to predict the probable cost in succeeding years. The material purchased by these funds will be very limited and sufficient, as I have already emphasized, for research purposes only.
In order to have a supply of ACTH for assay purposes, the food and drug laboratories of the Department of National Health and Welfare have made arrangements with Canada Packers of Hull for enough hog pituitary glands for [DOT] the preparation in Ottawa of very limited quantities of ACTH.
2970	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Health and Welfare The product of this federal laboratory will be tested for potency and stability against preparations of known strength prepared in Chicago and Toronto. It will then be assigned a potency value and retained as a reference standard for the testing of preparations from all manufacturers. This work is being directed by Dr. L. I. Pugsley, chief of the laboratory services in the food and drug division, who in 1933 worked with Dr. J. B. Collip, then professor of biochemistry at McGill university, on some of the first studies made of ACTH. This Ottawa project is the immediate responsibility of W. D. Snair, who has had considerable experience in the preparation and assay of ACTH, having taken his M.Sc. degree in this branch of endocrinology at the university of Toronto.
The development of ACTH and cortisone is an outstanding example of international co-operation in medical research, and of the value of the free interchange of scientific information. It is a notable fact that although the first regular production of both ACTH and cortisone has taken place in the United States, Canadian scientists have been kept fully advised and are co-operating in this undertaking. For several months we have received progress reports from the officers of our department, and also from Canadian scientists who have attended meetings of the committee of the National Academy of Science in Washington that was established to correlate information in this field. We have also established liaison with those who perhaps can be described as mainly responsible for the development of these new drugs.
Early in the 1920's American research scientists demonstrated that the functioning of the adrenal cortex is under the influence of the anterior pituitary, a tiny gland controlling growth and sexual development as well as influencing the functioning of the adrenal and thyroid glands. In 1933 Dr. J. B. Collip, one of our outstanding research men, then at McGill and now dean of medicine at the university of Western Ontario, demonstrated that what had been believed to be a single, simple hormone from the anterior pituitary gland could be broken up into fractions to perform several functions. One of these fractions is ACTH.
In this work Dr. Collip was assisted by Dr. Evelyn Anderson, now in the United States public health service, and Dr. D. L. Thomson, now dean of graduate studies and research at McGill university. The first report of these studies was published in the English medical journal, the Lancet, in', "
August 1933. Dr. Hans Selye, also working at McGill at this time, who is now head of the institute of experimental medicine and surgery at the university of Montreal, devised a practical method of removing the minute pituitary glands in animals used for experimental purposes.
Three years later, Dr Selye first announced his theory-which is of great interest-about the body's defensive mechanisms against injury and disease and the way in which they involve the pituitary-adrenal linkage.
It was not until several years later that- at about the same time-Dr. C. H. Li and Dr. H. M. Evans of the university of California and Drs. Sayers, White and Long of Yale university, obtained purified ACTH from the anterior pituitary glands of sheep and swine. Dr. Long also worked at McGill university for some years.
In 1947, J. B. Fishman of Yale university developed a method of preparing ACTH which gave yields considerably higher than those obtained by previous workers, and last year Dr. Li's work opened up the possibility of synthesizing ACTH. Also in 1948, Dr. J. S. L. Browne, professor of medicine at McGill university, and his associates carried out studies on the metabolic effects of ACTH on the human system.
As yet it is beyond the powers of scientists to produce these drugs in quantity. Efforts are being made to find better sources or less complicated and time-consuming production methods. Meanwhile, we are ensuring that funds will be available in Canada to further all useful lines of investigation both into the production and the use of these drugs. To do this we must resolutely conserve them exclusively for research purposes as this is the surest guarantee of shortening the time that must elapse-and it might be a very long time-before they can be made available for all that they can benefit.
I have made this statement in collaboration, of course, with the officers of my department, but also in collaboration with some of the men whose names I have mentioned and who have deemed it necessary to state some of the things I have said. I have done so because of the great importance attached to cortisone and ACTH by leading authorities in Canada, and indeed all over the world. The considerable resources of Canadian scientific research are now being mobilized to ensure a worth-while Canadian contribution in a matter so important to humanity.
Item stands.
Progress reported."]

speechtext:
Press dispatches of yesterday, December 7, indicate that there was a vote in the United Nations concerning Southwest Africa. As I read the dispatches, a resolution was put through asking the international court of justice to rule on the status of Southwest Africa. That resolution was bitterly opposed by South Africa but was carried; and I believe Canada supported the motion. There may have been good reasons for that action on Canada's part, tout the minister should explain them to the committee. South Africa is a sister nation in the commonwealth. Over a period of years she has been severely criticized by some nations which really have not much right to criticize, because they do not deal with their own problems any better than South Africa has dealt with hers; and I believe some nations at least have been very unfair in the attitude they have adopted toward our sister nation. South Africa is facing a very difficult problem in Southwest Africa, and it is all too easy for these other nations to throw bricks at her.
Personally I rather regret that Canada joined with the other nations in voting against South Africa on a question of this kind, which must make things very awkward for that country. One has only to think back


to the meeting in San Francisco, where Field Marshal Smuts was one of the key men in bringing about the organization of the United Nations. If it had not been for his wise leadership perhaps there would have been no United Nations organization. In other years he has been attacked personally before that assembly; and now, this week, we have this further attack on South Africa in which Canada joined with these other countries. I should like the minister to give us some explanation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think there is some misunderstanding in the mind of the hon. gentleman as to what we actually did, that is what the Canadian delegation did at Lake Success, on this matter. We have had close and very friendly co-operation with the South African delegation at the assembly. As the committee is aware, that delegation was under attack because of certain alleged inadequacies in its policies with regard to Southwest Africa.
We did not support certain efforts made by other delegations to impose obligations upon the Union of South Africa in respect of this territory which we thought she was not obliged to accept under the charter, but there was some doubt whether the obligation of supplying information to the United Nations on behalf of that territory rested with South Africa, and we supported a resolution to refer that and related matters to the international court to obtain a legal opinion as to whether South Africa was under an obligation to submit that information to the United Nations. That is all we did in that regard, and in the circumstances I do not think the South African delegation would quarrel with our attitude on that resolution.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then the press dispatch is wrong. According to it there were two votes. The first was on a motion to have the international court of justice rule on the status of Southwest Africa, and the report says Canada voted for that motion. Is the newspaper report correct?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I have not seen the newspaper report, nor as yet have I seen the official report from our delegation, which will probably arrive today. We did vote for a resolution to submit to the international court the question of South Africa's obligations in respect of Southwest Africa, whether it is or is not analogous to a trust territory. All we wanted to do by that vote was to have this question cleared up by a legal opinion. We may have abstained on the other question,

as to whether South Africa should or should not supply the United Nations with certain information; but if we did abstain, as I see it, that would not necessarily mean a judgment on South Africa's policy. One reason we may have abstained in regard to whether South Africa should or should not supply certain information would be that we felt it might be undesirable to take a definite position in that regard until we knew what was South Africa's legal position in regard to Southwest Africa.

speechtext: If Canada abstained from voting on the resolution asking for further information about Southwest Africa, why on earth should she vote for the resolution asking the international court of justice to go into the question of the status of Southwest Africa?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Since July 1, 1947, when IRO began its work, some 260,000 refugees have been resettled, some of them in their own countries of origin, some in other European countries and others in countries abroad. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

In the return which was brought down in my name and also in the evidence to which the minister referred, I noticed that certain expenses incurred in connection with displaced persons coming to Canada are met out of IRO funds. My experience with this has been that in some instances they have been paid, and in a great many instances they have not been paid. In my own constituency I know of two instances at least where the sponsors had to pay as high as $900 and $1,000 in order to bring displaced persons, refugees, to this country. In that connection I should like to ask two questions.
Since there are, or are presumed to be, a number of organizations in Canada which contact the sponsors of displaced persons and ask for certain amounts of money to be paid before these persons can come out, will the minister give us a list of what might be regarded as legitimate organizations which are now contacting the relatives of displaced persons and asking them for the payment of certain amounts of money before these persons can come out? Is there any method by which those who have paid these large sums of money can secure refunds? It seems most unfair when you take two cases. In the one case the bulk of the expenses have been paid, and in the other case none of the expenses have been paid even though it worked great hardship on the sponsor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Displaced persons?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: All displaced persons coming to this country under the auspices of that organization are treated in the same way. There may well be, however, other displaced persons who find their way to Canada in other ways, and I am not sure what the situation is in regard to the payment of their travelling expenses. The IRO does pay the travelling expenses of the people under its jurisdiction coming to Canada. I shall be glad to look into that and see if there are organizations of the kind the hon. member suggests, and find out whether injustices have been done through the activities of those organizations whereby some displaced persons get their expenses paid and others do not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I would certainly appreciate an investigation. The individual sponsor has no way of knowing whether an organization is legitimate or not; and of course they are so keen about getting those people out that they will sacrifice to the limit. I know of cases where it has occurred in order to get enough
Supply-External Affairs money to meet the demands of the organization. I certainly hope this matter will be looked into.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
May I just say a word on this? I think the Department of Labour and the Department of Immigration ought to be commended on the manner in which they have dealt with this question of displaced persons in the last two years. One should express appreciation of the manner in which this has been dealt with latterly. For a year or two we were prone to complain that Canada was not doing her part in giving refuge to those who had suffered from nazi oppression and the threat of communist retaliation if they were returned to their countries of origin.
I have had something to do with the setting up of the IRO and have had considerable correspondence with the department in regard to people, particularly from the Baltic states, whom I regard as very desirable settlers in this country. I have found that the Department of Labour and our representatives overseas have given every attention to any request that has been made.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. member, I wonder whether it is because persons who wished to bring relatives and displaced persons had been, shall I say, sufficiently ill advised to accept approaches by certain people offering to bring relatives over for a consideration. I came across an instance in my own constituency a short time ago of an approach from Paris, as a matter of fact, in connection with the coming of the mother of a gentleman in my constituency. The amount asked for was $1,000. Fortunately the man who had been in contact with the people in Paris asked me about it when I was out there last summer. I said: "Don't send the $1,000. I shall inquire of our own department." I inquired in the department and the department made inquiries overseas. The result was that the necessary order in council was passed. The money for the passage of this lady from Germany to Canada has been paid to the Canadian National Railways and I have no doubt that if she can get out of Poland she will arrive here at a fraction of the cost that was originally asked.
As far as possible people should be advised to get in touch with responsible government officials or organizations, and get advice before they pay out large sums of money to get people into this country. As I understand, there is no need for them to do that. If the person is in a displaced persons camp the IRO looks after it. If they are not in such a camp the thing to do is to get in touch with the Canadian National or the Canadian
2928	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs Pacific or one of the transportation organizations and the department, get the necessary permission, and the cost will be a fraction of what is asked.
I rose to say I have appreciated the co-operation of the department and the manner in which they have in the last two years at least endeavoured to work out the settlement of displaced persons and particularly the persons who I think can make a contribution to this country. However, I must add this. There is growing in the displaced persons camps a hard corps of persons who are not easily integrated, shall I say, into the life of the various countries. Because of war disabilities some of them have become deafened. For example, I know of a Latvian family where two of the children were deafened in an air raid by the British forces on a German city and the parents cannot come without them. On the other hand, I understand, this country is hesitant about bringing them in, or perhaps some people who have contracted lung trouble or something of that sort because they were refugees running away from the oppression of Hitler, or if it was in the Baltic states, from the Russians when they came in. They have suffered in the common cause, and perhaps I might suggest to the minister that some attention should be given to seeing whether the nations together can come to an arrangement whereby perhaps at least some of these people can be taken care of in our country. Indeed, perhaps if we erected institutions for some of these people, in years to come those institutions might be very valuable to this country in the field of public health.
I know it is a difficult problem, but I feel that as a Christian country, and actuated as most people in this country are by humanitarian principles, we should consider those who are not as physically fit as others we have taken to assist us in the performance of various types of labour in this country.
I am speaking to the minister on behalf of these unfortunate people in the camps in Europe.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see this appropriation in the estimates. The people in Canada have shown their interest in this fund because when last April an appeal was made a very considerable sum

of money was raised voluntarily, as well as a contribution of some $6 million which I believe has been made to this organization.
I do not believe there is anything which can create more good will for this country and the other countries participating in the fund than can this international children's emergency fund. These children are helped wherever they may be, in any and every country. While it may be said that children are being helped in countries unfriendly to us, nevertheless I believe that when the children in those countries grow up they will appreciate what has been done for them, not only in the matter of providing food and clothing to meet their present distress, but also in the medical care and the treatment given them to make them useful world citizens.
I have always been interested in seeing this sort of thing undertaken, not only by private organizations-and I believe we should use private organizations as well-but, when the need is as great as it is now, by nations making contributions from the public purse. I am glad Canada is doing that.
Perhaps on another occasion I may point out the need of doing something for our own children in our own country. But the fact that we have to do so is no reason why we should not participate in a worth-while international fund to help children throughout the world. It is true that charity begins at home; but there is another part of the good book which says that if we cast our bread upon the waters it will return to us after many days. I think this is one way of casting bread upon the waters, and I am sure that one day we shall be rewarded tenfold for what we are trying to do now.

speechtext: 455. Canals service, administration, $81,400.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I shall not take up much time in discussing the estimates of this very important department. So far as the maritime provinces are concerned this department is most important. We have already had some discussion with respect to the transport board. The other night the hon, member for Charlotte made a scathing denunciation of trading relations with central Canada and of present government policy, and condemned the present situation as between the maritime provinces and central Canada. This is remarkable when one considers that this government has been in office continuously, with the exception of the depression years, since 1921. It might be worth while for me to read what the hon. member for Charlotte said, as reported on page 2785 of Hansard:
I often wonder if the people of Ontario and Quebec realize just exactly the position we are in down in the maritimes. There is nothing that we have to offer that they want in central Canada. We are obliged to go to our neighbours to the south of us in order to sell our products. But when we bring that money back into Canada, if there is anything that we might want for our homes we have to go to Ontario and pay two prices for it.
That is a serious denunciation of the government's policies as they affect the maritimes. The freight rates with central Canada are excessive and it is most difficult for the producers of natural products in the maritime provinces to get their goods to the markets of central Canada. I am not going to follow that up except to point out that this matter is exceedingly important to the maritime provinces and we are not satisfied with what has been done by the government, by the minister or his predecessors in order to make it more profitable for us to trade with central Canada and attain that measure of prosperity we should have.
I am going to take a few minutes to refer to canals, to the Chignecto canal. The building of this canal has been before this house ever since confederation. The hon. member for Royal has brought it up recently, as well as the hon. member for Queens and the hon. member for Gloucester. This session it was brought up by the hon. member for Saint-John-Albert, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough and other hon. members.

Supply-Transport
A committee has been set up in the maritime provinces to press for the construction of this canal. Many agree with me, that there is sufficient information in the hands of the department to permit them to announce a policy for the construction of this canal. We heard yesterday, and again today, oft repeated reference to the St. Lawrence canal. Everyone in central Canada seems to be straining at the leash to get that canal and power development under way. More than $350 million has been expended in central Canada on canals, and though the Chignecto canal was promised to us from the days of confederation, nothing has yet been done for us.
The minister has had this matter brought repeatedly to his personal attention and I am going to ask him to make an announcement today. I base this request on the premise that it is due to the maritime provinces, that it will have strategic defence value, that it will be commercially worth while and will provide needed employment as well. There should be sufficient information on the records to show that it is feasible. Engineers report possibilities of large power development.
I should like the minister to state what the government proposes to do in connection with the construction of this canal. If the minister states that he has not sufficient surveying and engineering data available, competent men should be appointed by the federal government and recommended by this Chignecto canal committee, which has been doing such good work in the maritime provinces. We would then know where we were. A declaration of policy should be made immediately by the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: A couple of weeks ago I asked the minister what progress has been made on the Canso project and he promised to make a statement on his estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
That item is considerably down on the list and perhaps I shall say something on it when we reach the item. With all the respect that is due to the committee I should like to remind it that this is the third day we have had the estimates of the Department of Transport before us. If there is to be a full discussion, of course I am prepared to answer all questions, but I should like to draw that fact to the attention of the committee at this time.
The hon. member for Cumberland made certain statements with regard to transportation generally and I am sorry that I must disagree entirely and fully with what he said about the manner in which transportation services in the maritime provinces are handled. I am sorry that I have not the

The chief matter with which the hon. member seems to be concerned at the moment is the building of the Chignecto canal. Supply-Transport
On November 21 the Minister of Trade and Commerce read a report, on behalf of the Minister of Transport, who was not present at the time, giving what purported to be a summary of the findings of the Kellock commission in regard to the Noronic tragedy. At page 1991 of Hansard for November 21, I find that the following are the opening words in the presentation of the report:
I wish to give the house a summary of the report of the court of investigation into the loss of the steamship Noronic by fire on September 17 last.
What follows is a summary which was read to the house and appears in the record. In the report there was reference at a number of places to the outstanding examples of negligence which had contributed in some way to what took place. At one point I find these words:
Moreover, complete complacency had descended upon both the ship officers and the management. The fire which actually occurred found officers and crew without any organization designed to deal with such a situation.
I do not suggest that these words in any way failed to interpret correctly the situation which existed so far as the shipowners, officers and management are concerned as it appeared from the evidence. But there is one consideration which I think should be in the minds of hon. members. This was one of the most important statements made to the house during the present session. A tragedy had occurred which shocked not only members of the house, but every Canadian, and I imagine also every citizen of the United States who read of that disastrous fire and its appalling consequences. For this reason special significance attaches to this report, because everyone is concerned about the possibility and the danger of fire. No one with a sense of responsibility would refuse to do everything possible to prevent tragedies that result from fire breaking out where human beings are in a position of danger. It was essential, therefore, that a balanced picture of what was contained in the report should be presented to the members of this house, and, through the reporting of proceedings here, to the people of Canada.
What actually was not contained in the summary was a very important part of the findings of that report. When the summary used the expression that "complete complacency had descended upon both the ship officers and the management", it should have added that the report made it clear that complete complacency had descended upon the inspection staff of the Department of Transport, which was charged with this responsibility.
None of us here has any desire to direct unpleasant criticism at anyone, but we would

not be doing our duty if we did not make sure that all the lessons to be gained from this report are placed before the members of the house and the people of Canada. Such a summary as was presented to hon. members, purporting to give a balanced picture of a finding of this kind, should have contained every essential consideration that might be in the minds of those who read it. That, I must say, is not my interpretation of this summary as I compare it with the report of the court of investigation set up by the minister under Mr. Justice Kellock, acting as commissioner.
On page 9 of the report, under the heading "Legislation, including regulations", I find these words:
Before dealing with the actual events of the night in question, it is relevant to consider the background of legislation and regulations to which the ship and its owners were subject.
Then the report goes on to deal with fire-resistant bulkheads, and says:
Under the provisions of section 405 (1) (a) of the Canada Shipping Act, regulations were passed on the 7th of July, 1939.
It goes on to review certain regulations in regard to bulkheads, and on page 10 I find
these words:
The Noronic was built in 1913 and had been constructed without any fire-resisting bulkheads. She was not required to comply with the provisions of regulation 47, the exemption taking the form of a certificate stating that the ship had complied with the regulations.
I want to repeat that sentence:
She was not required to comply with the provisions of regulation 47, the exemption taking the form of a certificate stating that the ship had complied with the regulations. There is nothing in the records of the board as to the reason for this decision but the evidence indicates that other existing ships were similarly treated. As far as the Noronic is concerned, it was not impracticable, on the evidence, to install fire-resisting bulkheads in accordance with the regulations. It must therefore be assumed that the chairman considered that, from the standpoint of expense, it would be unreasonable to require compliance.
I do not intend to extend my remarks on that point beyond saying that when the parliament of Canada passes certain laws imposing certain responsibilities, and employees in the service of Canada are entrusted with the duty of carrying out those laws and the regulations thereunder, where danger to human life is involved no official in the public service of Canada has the right to take upon himself the responsibility of saying that, because of cost, safety measures which are clearly laid down shall not be complied with. This is simply another evidence of the tendency to suspend the law being carried from government to officials of government. It is not something that stands by itself alone; it is evidence of a tendency we have seen in other cases as well.

On page 16, after devoting several pages to the whole question of inspection, the report contains these words:
The government inspector, who inspected the ship annually, and his superior, were of opinion that if two hydrants on a particular deck were not sufficiently close to a particular point to enable two separate hoses to be brought to bear on such a locality, the regulation would be satisfied if it would be possible to bring a hose from the deck above or the deck beneath. In practice this had never been done at any fire drill and, in my opinion, such an operation should not have been relied on . . .
Then on page 17-and all this part deals with the question of regulations, inspections, and compliance with the law-I see these words:
As to regulation 6, which deals with the provision for making available two powerful jets of water in the coal bunker spaces, boiler rooms and engine rooms, there was only one hydrant capable of supplying a single hose in the engine room and boiler rooms. The inspector said in evidence that in that situation he could not say that regulation had been complied with, although the certificate which he issued to the owners states that the statute had been complied with.
In other words, according to the evidence of the inspector he could not actually substantiate an important certificate which stated that a statute, upon which human safety depended, had been complied with.
Again, after reviewing the subject further, and going into further details of safety measures which were not carried out, I come to these words on page 18:
The inspection consisted of lifting up each extinguisher for the purpose of seeing whether or not it had been charged and in turning two or three upside down to ascertain if they would operate. It was impossible for the inspector therefore to say, from such an inspection, that the requirements of the regulation as to the provision of the necessary number of extinguishers "in each enclosed space occupied by passengers or crew" on each deck, had been satisfied. Such an inspection does not attain the real purpose of the regulation, namely, that a sufficient number of fire extinguishers ready for instant use shall be in position on each deck.
Then, in a discussion of the subject of pumps, I come to these words in the report:
The Noronic, at the time of the fire, had complied with this regulation as to the number of pumps, but all three considered by the inspector as complying with the regulation were in fact "fitted in the same space," contrary to the express provision of the regulation.
By virtue of the fact that they were fitted in the same space, they did not comply with the regulation. I am going to refer to the next page in a moment, but I want to point out that this review of the regulations and the failure to enforce them appears in the report before the general discussion of the failure of the management and officials to carry out their responsibilities. I believe that it must be the opinion of most if not all of
Supply-Transport
the members of the house that those inspections and those standards which are imposed under the laws passed by parliament must be the starting point of those measures of safety which we expect to be enforced in ships, vehicles or anything else carrying human beings. The attitude of the commissioner as to the effect of this failure by the inspector and others to insist upon compliance with the regulations is clearly indicated in these words found at page 20 of the report, and this is in regard to smoke helmets and safety lamps:
I venture to think that the laxity in the particulars mentioned above in requiring compliance with the regulations could only induce or encourage a similar laxity on the part of the owners and officers of the ship with respect to the vital matter of preparedness for fire.
Those words come at the end of the review of the various regulations and the failure to insist upon compliance with them. It indicates that the commissioner was clearly of the opinion that the failure to insist upon compliance with those regulations by the inspector and other officials had not only made possible a disaster of this kind but had actually induced or encouraged a similar laxity on the part of the owners and officers of the ship.
Let us see what happened to those concerned where there had been laxity. We had read into the records of the house the decision by the court that the captain of the ship lost his right to command that ship as a result of his laxity, and there can be no doubt about the measure of responsibility upon the shipowners and management, through the evidence of laxity there. But surely when the commissioner appointed by the minister to carry out the provisions of an act of this parliament, and to report to this parliament, says that the laxity of the government official actually induced or encouraged the laxity that was reported to the house, then I think we should have known that fact at the same time. But in any event, now that we know of it, we should insist that the laxity of the government official shall be dealt with with the same severity that was regarded as necessary for the prevention of similar accidents in other cases in the future.
We have a civil service of which we have every reason to be proud; but the standards of that civil service will not be maintained or elevated by any suggestion that civil servants are not subject to the same standards and the same tests of responsibility as are those whom they must instruct in the requirements under any act passed by this parliament. If under the laws passed by the parliament of Canada certain penalties are imposed upon others for laxity, then it will be in keeping with our attitude toward the standards of our civil service to make sure

Supply-Transport
that a similar attitude is adopted where laxity of this kind induced other laxity which produced tragedy such as that which occurred in this case. There was no mention of that matter in the report; but on December 3, some time after we were given the information, a Canadian Press dispatch was reported in the press. It gave no names of any people who had been dealt with but it stated:
A transport department steamship inspection official has been reprimanded by transport minister Chevrier as a result of the Noronic fire, it was learned today.
The official came before Mr. Chevrier who rebuked him for "laxity" in signing the certificate which allowed the vessel to ply lake waters.
I do not think that the laxity which the commissioner, Mr. Justice Kellock, said was a laxity that induced and encouraged the other laxity which resulted in tragedy is dealt with sufficiently by a rebuke.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: May I inform my hon. friend immediately that, contrary to what is stated in the report read by my hon. friend, no inspector came before me nor was any inspector rebuked by me in connection with laxity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: From that do I take it that no action has been taken?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then I think that is exceedingly serious.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: You may not take that from it. But when a report is read by an hon. gentleman in this chamber, and the report is not even anywhere near the truth, then surely the person who is alleged to have made it can say whether he made it or not. I repeat that on no occasion did there come before me an inspector of the steamship inspection branch of the department who was rebuked. I will deal with what was done when I reply; but that is the position with regard to the press release read by my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I think it would perhaps facilitate a discussion of this matter, Mr. Chairman, if the minister would say whether he has taken steps to deal with the laxity reported in this case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I will deal with that in a moment, if I may.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
If that is so, then I will defer my further remarks until I have heard what actually happened; because there is a report there by the commissioner which should have been placed before the house but which was not placed before the house in the summary that was read. We have the report, it is true; and on reading that report we find what the

facts are. On the basis of the recommendations of the commissioner, I think it is quite clear that action in regard to the failure of the government official or officials to deal with this matter was clearly indicated, and I for one should like to hear what action was taken.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think the committee will agree that a tragedy such as that which happened at the Canada Steamship Lines dock in the city of Toronto is one which is so serious that not the slightest attempt should be made by any hon. gentleman in the committee or elsewhere to make capital of it in any sense of the word. In saying that, I am not suggesting that that is what my hon. friend had in mind; in fact, I feel that such is not the case. But I wish to make the statement that the tragedy was of such a nature that we should approach both the report and the recommendations in the light of the evidence that came before the commissioner.
I think my hon. friend stated that, in the statement read to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, while much was made of the laxity of the owners and the captain, nothing was said about the laxity of the steamship inspection. Am I correct in that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: What I said was that the laxity was duly reported in regard to the steamship owners and the captain but that, so far as I am aware, it is not in regard to the officials who dealt with them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The report which I have before me, and which were the notes read by the Minister of Trade and Commerce-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: What date was that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The exact date to which my hon. friend referred. The report contained a very express reference to steamship inspection. On the fourth page of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce I find these words:
The commissioner expresses the opinion that the laxity of the inspection in requiring compliance with the regulations could only induce or encourage a similar laxity on the part of the owners and officers of the ship with respect to the vital matter of preparedness for fire.
My hon. friend says that there was no reference-or at least that is the purport that I took from his remarks-in the statement made by my colleague to the laxity of the officer in the division of steamship inspection.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
There is no summary of the details in the report in that respect. There may be reasons for that. But I do want to point out that what I read was a reference

to the complacency which had descended- and which I said had obviously also occurred to the commissioner-upon the department, and that that should have been brought in in a balanced report which would clearly indicate the relationship-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
There is clear reference to that in the statement made by the minister. In any event, the report was tabled in the house. The report is a lengthy one and evidently it would not be possible to make a statement covering all of the facts and all of the circumstances that were contained in it.
My hon. friend has dealt with some of the statements contained in the report and has read from some of the evidence in the report; but he omitted some that have a very material bearing. For instance, I refer to that part dealing with fire-resisting bulkheads, and the exemption which, under the regulations, the chairman of the steamship inspection board has the discretion to grant in a particular case. The report goes on to say that the regulation providing for fire-resisting bulkheads was made in 1939, and steamship inspection decided that it would not be practical to make the regulation retroactive to ships which were then in existence. That is a practice which exists not only in Canada but in the United States. I am informed it is the practice that exists all over the world. When new regulations are made dealing with technical changes of this importance, having to do with steamship inspection, rarely if ever are they made retroactive. Therefore, what the chairman of steamship inspection was doing on that particular occasion he was doing in conformity with what I am informed had been done in most countries of the world and in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to interrupt, but what it says on page 10 is:
As far as the Noronic is concerned, it was not impracticable, on the evidence, to install fire-resisting bulkheads in accordance with the regulations. It must therefore be assumed that the chairman considered that, from the standpoint of expense, it would be unreasonable to require compliance.
That is a very different reason.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Not at all. The point which I am making is that this regulation applied to ships other than the Noronic.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
And ships in the same position as the Noronic in so far as putting that regulation into force was concerned. Notwithstanding that, they were exempted from the operation of that regulation, and they were exempted for the reason that I gave a
Supply-Transport
moment ago. I am not going to say wisely, because of the recommendation made by the commissioner. But nonetheless the Noronic cannot be pointed out as being an exception, because all other similar passenger ships were exempted from that regulation.
My hon. friend went on to read from pages of the report concerning fire extinguishers and fire extinguishing equipment. May I draw to the attention of my hon. friend what the commissioner said at the end of the first paragraph on page 17. He said:
In any event, it does not appear that the failure to extinguish the fire at a stage when that would have been possible, was due to any deficiency in the number of location of hydrants.
Dealing with the same subject the commissioner said at the end of the page:
Again, it should be said, however, that noncompliance with this regulation did not prejudice the situation at the time of the fire.
He deals with the steamship inspector, the very inspector, the only inspector from the steamship division, who gave evidence as to the actual inspection of that ship. He condemns that inspector because of the fact that instead of going about the ship and examining the hydrants, the fire extinguishing equipment, the helmets, et cetera, the inspector collected them all on the deck, examined them there and gave a certificate just as if they had been examined on the spot.
In giving the report which he did I believe that the steamship inspector was not stating the facts as they were, and in that respect he was guilty of laxity. Let me tell my hon. friend that the commissioner deals with him and him alone because there was no other person who gave evidence on the actual examination, save and except another officer from steamship inspection 'who gave evidence on the regulations and who is not singled out in this particular report.
Dealing with the pumps and with the evidence of that inspector to whom I referred a moment ago the commissioner states at the bottom of page 19:
It cannot be said, however, on the evidence before me, that the location of the pumps in breach of the regulation was the cause of this failure.
There is only one place in his report, and that is on page 20, where the commissioner refers to the laxity in the particulars above referred to as read by my hon. friend. The recommendations are there. They are too numerous to read at this time. They are there and can be read, but I do not want to take up the time of the committee unduly. They contain no recommendation in so far as the inspection division of the Department of Transport is concerned. They contain a number of other

Supply-Transport
recommendations; and here I can tell the committee that at no time did I ask Inspector Craig to come before me, nor did I reprimand him. What I did was to call before me the deputy chairman of the steamship inspection branch. I discussed with him the regulations and the recommendations. I indicated to him certain parts of the report, particularly that part on page 20, which had to do with laxity, and which was directed at one man and one man alone. I cannot for one moment concede that a conclusion based upon the evidence of one individual could be directed at other individuals who were not examined and who did not give evidence before the court of inquiry. So that the position I am taking and the point I am making now is that condemnation of the commissioner, in so far as laxity is concerned, is directed at one man, that individual who gave evidence on that occasion and who inspected the Noronic.
My information is that the inspector is a man of some years. I discussed with the deputy chairman of the steamship inspection board the question of his position. In view of the fact that the man is about to retire, and has reached the retiring age-in fact I believe he has gone beyond the retiring age- it was decided that no action would be taken by way of dismissal. But the contents of the report have not yet been fully considered in so far as the recommendations are concerned, because I have not yet come to the conclusion whether or not it will be necessary to bring in legislation, or whether or not this report can be implemented in another way.
In any event I can assure the house that no one realizes the seriousness of the position any more than my officials and I do. I have no hesitation in announcing that the recommendations of the commissioner will be put into effect just as quickly as that is possible, in order that tragedies of this sort or fires of this kind be not repeated in our country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, no one will wish to see anyone suffer unnecessarily; but the finding is inescapable by the commissioner, on evidence which he regarded as adequate-and he is a most experienced judge-that the laxity in the various particulars which he mentioned, and to which I referred by quotations indicating the nature of the findings, could only induce or encourage similar laxity on the part of the owners and officers of the ship.
The fact that the minister has just explained that what occurred in connection with the Noronic was not an exception, but that similar situations existed in other ships as well, merely emphasizes that the necessity for inspection is one of the features emerging

from this report, and that it is essential that in future there be certainty from the administrative point of view that the provisions for inspection and supervision shall be strictly adhered to.
While it is true that in one case there was a discretionary provision, there were other cases where certificates were given which really stated something which in one instance the witness knew nothing about or was not sure about, and in the other case the witness made a statement contrary to actual fact.
Those matters do require the most vigorous attention. Even without new statutory provisions, this report certainly emphasizes the necessity for the utmost vigour in dealing with this particular matter.
I wish to make it clear-and I believe the record of my remarks will bear this out- that I said I did not suggest that there was any misinterpretation of the actual finding, but that I would emphasize the complacency that had descended upon the management and those charged with the direction of the ship, and the fact also that it should have been brought home to us that such complacency had apparently existed at a point where it induced the possibility of a situation of this kind.
I have nothing further to add to these remarks, beyond saying that I welcome the assurance that the report will be acted upon. I do feel also that in cases of this kind, where human life is possibly in jeopardy if the regulations are not complied with, the most severe standards should be required from those whose actions will determine the actions of those whose activities are inspected.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
While this disaster occurred on the great lakes, it has been one of great concern to people on the west coast, because we travel extensively by ship. I am greatly concerned about the minister's statement to the effect that when these new regulations to ensure safety become operative they are not to be made applicable to ships already built. If that rule is strictly followed it means that only those ships built after the time the regulations come into effect will be subject to these safety measures.
It is obvious from the Noronic disaster that if that ship had been forced to comply with the new regulations there would have been no tragedy. Had the regulations been made to apply to the ships already plying the great lakes it is not likely the tragedy would have occurred. I hope the department will not take the stand that safety regulations enacted in the future need not apply to ships already in operation. Certainly these safety measures

should be made to apply to all ships. I should like to have some further word from the minister on that point.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he made his statement, indicated that there would be some sort of investigation into the question of whether there should be amendments to the Canada Shipping Act and other legislation, and whether changes should be made in the regulations. Will the Minister of Transport tell us what steps are being taken to investigate those two points? Is there some body within his department reviewing the statutes and regulations, or is there to be some body outside the Department of Transport? Will representations be heard from the various bodies across the country which are interested in the safety of ships at sea? If there is some group, departmental or otherwise, investigating the act and the regulations, provision should be made for representations from across the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Dealing first with that part of my hon. friend's remarks which dealt with ships on the Pacific coast, my reply would be that our steamship inspection service following this report has been given instructions to make a complete investigation of all ships on the west coast, for safety purposes, and to make sure that the steamship inspection regulations are enforced. That is being done at the moment. Part of it has been done this week and the rest of it will be done early next week. My hon. friend has said that if the regulations with regard to fire-resistant bulkheads had been put into force there would have been no fire.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I did not deal with any specific regulation. It seemed to me that if the regulations as they existed had been enforced with respect to the Noronic, even though she had been built before some of the regulations came into effect, it is quite probable there would have been no disaster. I am hitting at the failure to make the regulations apply to a ship built before they were brought in.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That is a difficult thing to say; that is conjecture.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I realize that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
One cannot say whether there would or would not have been a disaster, particularly when one is dealing with an act of God. One never knows when an act of God is going to occur, or under what circumstances or conditions. I venture to say, although this is also conjecture, that if this tragedy had taken place at sea the position would have been infinitely better. However, I do not want to get into a long discussion.
My hon. friend asked whether these regulations or the legislation would be made
Supply-Transport
retroactive. The regulation with regard to fire-resistant bulkheads on passenger ships has been in existence since 1939, but all passenger ships in the class of the Noronic were exempted at the discretion of the steamship inspection service. The commissioner recommends that fire-resistant bulkheads be installed in ships so that-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Even in the older ships.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Even in the older ships. If we carry out that recommendation it would meet the point raised by my hon. friend. With reference to changes in the Canada Shipping Act, there is a departmental committee which deals with changes to be made from time to time in the act. That committee will deal with these recommendations and any other changes that are likely to be made. It will consult from time to time with public bodies as to the necessity of making changes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Will an opportunity be given to make recommendations to that committee?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I would not say that. I remember the difficulty we got into with the C.S.U. when we amended the regulations before, but I will say that that committee will consult those who are interested, the shipowners and others.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: In changing the regulations the government should be careful that it is not starting on a witch-hunt. There are certain inherent risks in connection with travel by sea, air or rail. If changes are to be made in the regulation so that the older ships must instal fire-resistant bulkheads, I am sure that would be desirable but these things should be economical as well. Unless the fare-paying passengers are prepared to pay substantially higher rates, they will either go without steamship services or be ready to permit a degree of latitude to some operators.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member brought up that point. It has always been a fact in the Department of Transport that more requests are received for relaxing the regulations than for tightening them up; in fact I would say the ratio is almost 95 per cent to five in favour of relaxing the regulations. Because of this tragedy I do not think there is any other conclusion we can come to but that these will have to be enforced. However, this would apply only to passenger ships and in so far as they are concerned I do not think it will be too much of a hardship.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It is only natural that there would be more representations for relaxing the regulations because they would come from those who are operating the ships. The

Supply-Transport
passenger whose life is endangered because the regulations are not enforced is not in position to make representations to the minister. The people who have to travel on these ships have no way of knowing what the regulations are. The first thing they know there is a fire, a wreck occurs or there is carelessness of some kind which costs them their lives. After all, these regulations were not designed to help the operators; they were designed to save lives. I do hope that the minister and his department will see that proper regulations are prepared and that there is a careful official inspection of these ships.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The minister has referred to certain items in the report to indicate that the laxity of inspection in connection with the Noronic did not contribute to the disaster. There are a number of places in the report where that statement is made. I should like to direct attention to a paragraph on page 20 which deals with the question of laxity of inspection and non-compliance with the regulations.
I doubt if the minister or anyone else can estimate the extent to which the laxity of inspection which is quite evident from this report actually did contribute to the disaster that befell this ship. I have read the report carefully and have discussed it with a number of seamen sailing the great lakes. I agree with them when they say that, as far as the inspection reported here is concerned, the inspector referred to might just as well have been hired and paid by the shipowners. There is every indication here that the only persons being considered in that inspection were the shipowners. The inspection of pumps and fire hose and extinguishers, the enforcement of the regulations with regard to fire-resistant bulkheads and fire patrols, all seemed to be made in the interest of the shipowners.
I am sure many people in this country would feel much happier if they knew that these regulations and the whole matter of inspection were going to be tightened up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: A short time ago I asked the minister a question with regard to the regulations governing the number of people to be carried from Port aux Basques to Sydney and from Sydney to Port aux Basques. If new regulations have been enacted I shall have no more to say about this.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am informed that there is no difference in the regulations governing traffic one way or the other.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
If you will bear with me for a couple of minutes, may I say in that case the situation cannot have changed. I made a

trip up here on the 8th of September, and I do not mind going back tomorrow or the next day, but certainly if I have to come back again, as I likely will in the early months of the coming year, I am a little bit anxious about it. The situation is that there is a definite load limit on the boats for passengers from North Sydney to Port aux Basques, but the men on the ships tell me that there is no limit from Port aux Basques to North Sydney. I have seen people lying on the floor of the saloon and in the passageways. I have seen them seasick, and it is a most unpleasant sight. Not only is it unpleasant; the situation is definitely unsafe, and the officers of the ships are worried.
There is not sufficient lifeboat accommodation, and I am quite certain there would be a real tragedy if by any chance anything happened. I am not prepared to say who would be responsible. I merely draw the matter to your attention again. I think it is a most serious situation. I am not altogether speaking without some knowledge of it. As I informed the house before, I happen to be associated with the union that mans these ships, and the men and the masters are most worried about it. I feel that precautions should be taken as quickly as possible. I am sure the minister knows the matter to which I am referring.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has brought the situation to my attention. It is a matter of importance, and I will see that Canadian National Railways, who operate the service, are advised of it immediately.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: There is one other matter. It is rather difficult to try to talk about freight rates in Newfoundland when you are using ships and railways.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: May I remind the hon. member there are two items dealing specifically with freight rates.

speechtext: We can do that afterwards.

speechtext: Yes, if he will allow this item to pass.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I have two further questions which I am sure will not be controversial. I believe the minister will be able to answer them very readily under this item. What is the position as to the Clarenville boats? May we have a statement as to the question of future ownership? Does the C.N.R. propose to take them over? Primarily I am concerned in the one instance with the fact that the men who man these boats have been told they are not entitled to be regarded as pensionable. In other words, the boats are looked upon as being the property of the provincial government. They are operated by the C.N.R., and

the men on the boats have been told they will not be pensioned because they are not entitled to be regarded as members of the C.N.R. organization.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I can tell the hon. gentleman that the Clarenville boats, as already stated, are the property of the Newfoundland government. The dominion government has no intention of purchasing them. The Canadian National Railways operate one or two, or perhaps three, on a management fee basis for the government of Newfoundland, and so far as I know they do not intend to buy them.

Item agreed to.
462. Nautical service administration, $490,670.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Item 462 deals with the nautical service, and under that branch of the department training is given to merchant seamen. The branch also arranges for the distribution of war medals and memorial crosses to dependent relatives of merchant seamen who have lost their lives. Earlier in the session we had a discussion, in which both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Veterans Affairs were involved, concerning the present provision for vocational training for merchant seamen. As the order in council reads at the present time, the only men who were able to qualify were those who were under thirty years of age, and applications had to be made by the end of June of this year.
It has been pointed out that there were a great many men who were unable to qualify. As a matter of fact, I asked a question earlier in the session and received the reply that out of 770 applications which had been made only 321, less than half, had been able to qualify for training. I have no intention of going over the merits of the request for changed regulations. Both ministers know the picture.
When we were discussing the matter before I understood that active consideration was then being given to introducing an amendment to the order in council in order that more of these men might qualify. I think some of us urged that the age limit should be withdrawn. Each case has to be dealt with separately; in any event, there is wide discretion as to whether or not training should be given. We also urged that the deadline for applications should be lifted. I believe the Department of Veterans Affairs is so organized and equipped that it could carry on more extended vocational training. I should like to ask the Minister of Transport whether any change is to be made in the order in council.
Supply-Transport

Consideration has been given to that point. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am very glad to get that word from the minister. I should like to point out that the report of the Canadian maritime commission recommends a further drastic reduction in the Canadian merchant marine, which means there will be jobs at sea for fewer men, and consequently all the more need for vocational training.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The matter is being carefully considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I want to ask the minister again whether there is any possibility whatsoever of Newfoundland merchant seamen who served in war zones being brought within the class of people who received the 10 per cent bonus. they could not be applied to Newfoundland seamen. Any future order of course would take them in; but while I could give the matter consideration I would have little hope that those orders could be made retroactive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Would the minister give the matter serious consideration, because the situation arose only because they were not in the manning pool?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

I should like to take just a moment to say that I think it is in the national interest that the greatest possible use should continue to be made of the port of Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway. On a previous occasion I have mentioned the cattle that might be shipped through that port, and now I should like to read a letter in that connection. Recently I received this letter from the North Battle-ford board of trade.
Dear Mr. Bater:
We are in receipt of and thank you for your letter of November 25, with which you enclosed a copy of a letter you had addressed to Mr. P. J. Ibbotson, with regard to the establishment of a quarantine station for imported cattle, preferably at The Pas.
We believe Mr. Ibbotson has already left for Great Britain. It is our understanding that his intention is to import two carloads of registered Shorthorn cattle as the initial shipment, and that if this turns out to his satisfaction in all probability he will continue to import cattle.
