maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Just before we go on with item 484, may I ask the minister a question which may be a little bit off the Hudson Bay railway. Last year I noticed that Premier
Supply-Transport
Duplessis had announced that a railway would be constructed immediately-I think according to the newspaper report it was August 14, 1948-from a place called Havre St. Pierre opposite Anticosti island north to Allard lake. No application has come here for any rights or charter. I was wondering just what this railway was, what it is being built for and by whom.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That railway is being built for the purpose of a company known as the Kennecott Copper Company. Deposits of copper have been found in that area. The railway is twenty-seven miles long. The contract has been let to Fraser-Brace and it is purely a provincial railway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Is construction taking place?
Mr Chevrier: I think it is almost complete.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
In the house from time to time, in discussing the Hudson Bay railway, figures of 25 million to 40 million bushels have been mentioned as being tributary to that railway. I think all we have to do is to have a good look at the map of the west, and we will be inclined to think that all of the wheat in the province of Saskatchewan is tributary to the Hudson Bay railroad. I wonder if what is meant when the figure of 25 million bushels is mentioned is that that would be a goal at which to strive with regard to handling grain through the Hudson bay.
The season is short up there, we admit; but a couple of years ago I had occasion to talk to Mr. Peter Dalgleish, who is managing director of Dalgleish shipping lines, and he was of the opinion that the season might be lengthened quite a little bit with the help of an icebreaker in clearing ice from the mouth of the Churchill river and away from the elevators at the start of the season and also when the ice was beginning to form at the closing of the season. I should like the minister to give some attention to that suggestion. This afternoon we heard that an icebreaker was being built for use on the Atlantic coast and also for Hudson bay. I would think that in what might be considered the slack time for that icebreaker on the Atlantic and on the Hudson bay itself, it might well be used in helping to clear the ice from the port of Churchill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
All I can say is that the amount of wheat which was transported over the Hudson Bay railway this year amounted to 5,730,000 bushels. The railway is being used to fairly good capacity. There are some people who think that 25 million bushels should be carried by the railway. I do not know whether or not that can be done. I

Supply-Transport
am not in a position to say. But we are hopeful that more than the amount carried this year will be carried in the future.
As to extending the season of navigation, the position is that the season is about twelve to thirteen weeks in length and the question of providing an icebreaker in that area is one that has been given consideration from time to time; but I doubt whether it would be practical to use an icebreaker in the area. The department has been helpful through its national harbours board and through the Canadian National Railways, in assisting the Hudson Bay railway and particularly by reducing the insurance rates by about 25 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I think the facilities there can be extended to handle much more than 5 million or six million bushels. I was glad to hear the minister say that he has the same hopes as I have.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The progress of the Hudson Bay railway has been slow, at least in the eyes of those of us from the west who have been anxious to promote its use. The minister has heard my opinions on the subject on many previous occasions and I do not propose to make a speech now about the whole matter; but I should like to put before the committee and before him one or two ideas I have with regard to it.
I think that probably a good deal of the trouble is apathy on the part of many people and perhaps hostility on the part of a few. I do not make that latter statement rashly. I have been actively interested in this matter for five years and passively interested previous to that for a number of years. I know something about the problem. I have been up at the port. I have talked to the manager, to many people along the line, and to residents of Churchill itself. I do not like to say this, but I must do so. There is a persistent feeling-whether it be right or wrong

among the people in those areas which the railway might well serve, that there is somehow antagonism here in the east. I know I shall be accused of talking about the big interests and that sort of thing. I want to be reasonable in the matter, but it is true that most of our business operations, both financial and otherwise, are concentrated here in the east. Even in the matter of longshoremen who handle the grain for a few weeks when that port is open, these men are imported in some cases from the port of Montreal. Perhaps that is natural enough, because where you want to engage trained men, you must go to the place where the men are trained. I shall say no more about the matter, but that is a persistent feeling in the west; and it is well that the government should know it.
[Mr. Chevrler.l
I think one of the greatest disadvantages the port has to contend with is the fact that the marine insurance rate is too high. The insurance people are the last ones you would expect to do anything much about this matter because they can insure the cargoes for the present rate. It is not big business and naturally you would not expect them to get excited about lowering that rate. But there is no doubt in my mind, after making an exhaustive study of the matter, that that rate could be lowered. There are really three seasons in Churchill; I will not go into particulars, but one of the seasons is the season which exists in the minds of those insurance people. To my mind that season is much too short. I talked to a captain up there the last time I was at Churchill and he told me that in beautiful weather, in a calm sea with the sun shining, they lay for two days outside the borderline, wherever that is, whatever strait it is, at the mouth of the bay, and he said: We might just as well have been sailing in there, but we could not do so because we knew that if we did we would not be covered by insurance. He told me also that frequently there was a week or ten days after the insurance rate was removed that the port could have been used. I suggest, as I have suggested before in this chamber, that there should not be a fixed season in that particular case; I suggest that in this day and age, with our modern methods of predicting the weather, surely there could be a variation by which these dates could be settled, that the length of this season should not be inflexible as it is at the present time.
Another difficulty of course is storage of wheat in position, and when I say "in position" I mean in such position that such wheat could be profitably shipped out of that port. I know the situation was difficult during the war and since the war because there has been a tremendous demand for wheat. There has been a shortage of wheat and there has often been a necessity to get wheat out within certain time limits in order to meet certain contracts or to receive a certain price. But I suggest that perhaps, unfortunately, from what we have been hearing of late, that day seems to be past. I hope that if it is an ill wind, it will at least blow good to the port of Churchill and that from now on that position may be improved. At various times I have raised the matter of storage. It is a hard question about which to get information, but I am interested in it. We as a nation, or the wheat board if you like, must store wheat some place, and it does store wheat some place at almost all times of the year. It seems to me that there should be some way of storing it at Churchill. Of course the Churchill elevator holds only 2,500,000 bushels. I am

often amused by papers I see in the east. "Oh dear me", they say, " we could not store two and a half million bushels. Just think of keeping two and a half million bushels of wheat idle up there all that time." Think of what a small proportion the two and a half million bushels is to the immense wheat crop of this country. After all, it is only a drop in the bucket.
Then we have a great storage elevator built by the government and standing there in Saskatoon with a capacity of five and a half million bushels, none of which is ever used. I should not say "none". There are a few bushels of wheat in it; it may be a thousand or two but what is that compared to the five and a half million capacity? The only thing that I know that elevator has been good for in the last few years is that it has been used to store a few thousand bushels of rapeseed. It was held in that position so that it could be pressed for oil at the local wheat pool oil plant. I have suggested to the minister that flax might well have been stored there instead of being stored in the terminal elevators down here in the east, because there was a time when that small oil mill had to shut down because there was no flax there to be processed. At the same time there was lots of flax lying idle in the east upon which storage was being paid in these eastern elevators.
The storage of wheat is one of the difficulties of the situation, and I have suggested at least some remedy. Another tremendous difficulty-and I am not a grain man; I fail to understand this-is this diversion charge. The diversion charge is one of the most ridiculous things of which I have ever heard. The minister can correct me but I think it is 2| cents a bushel that we are charged in dealing with that wheat. What is a diversion charge? I am none too clear on it myself, but as far as I have discovered it appears to be a fee which is paid to certain grain companies for not handling wheat. In other words, if they had not the privilege of handling and storing that particular wheat then there is an assessment of 2| cents a bushel put against the wheat which is not so handled. That seems to me to be a ridiculous situation.
There are a great many people in my part of the country-and I think it includes all of the farmers in northern Saskatchewan- who are tremendously interested in this road and in the port. They look on it as their own road. Let me say here that you see various wild statements in the press that this white elephant thing was built at national expense. It was no such thing. It was built at the expense of the western provinces. They look
Supply-Transport
upon it as their own road. They are interested in it and they would like a little co-operation in making it a success. Great Britain has benefited from this route perhaps more than anybody else of recent years. As a nation Great Britain has benefited to the extent that she has been able to get wheat shipped out from Hudson bay. I think that helps our position in the British competitive market; and, if reports about our trade are true, assistance in that particular competitive market could be to our advantage some of these days.
This deficit, which is costing the taxpayers of this country money, is a thing in which business people in all parts of the country should be interested, one in which the taxpayers should be interested. The estimate calls for $50 million to square the deficit. This deficit, which must be met by the taxpayers, has been caused simply by one thing, namely, a lack of volume. I have a statement from the management of the port. I have statements from people in the grain trade. They estimate that a volume of fifteen million bushels would take care of the deficit. It would not make any profit, but it would mean that the taxpayers of the country would not have anything to pay in respect of this route.
I have pleaded that just once we ought to be able to get that much grain over this road and through this port in order to decide what is the value of this route. I have urged that business be sought for this road. I am afraid that I have always had the suspicion, held by many people in our part of the country, that business is not so sought. I have appealed to the minister that the railway might drum up some business. The Minister of Transport has told me that it is neither his business nor the railway's; that it is a matter for business institutions, and so forth. Still the minister has assured us that he was benevolent to the Churchill route, and I believe perhaps he still is. Yet we have not had the results that some of us would have desired, and which I think we might have expected. I will say this, that if there had been any interest in this country, if the Canadian National Railways had done the same amount of work in drumming up business as, for instance, the Dalgleish Shipping Company, which has shipped out most of the wheat from that port and shipped in most of the goods, if there had been some agencies in this country that had been working for the promotion of that port and road to the same extent that Mr. Dalgleish's company has, this thing would have been on a solid footing long before now.
I am aware of the influence that the wheat board has in this particular matter; I am

Supply-Transport
aware of the influence that the Minister of Trade and Commerce could have in this particular matter; and I am aware of the influence that the Minister of Transport could have. He will probably say that I am attributing to him powers which he has not. However, that is my own opinion on the matter.
As I said when I began, I do not want to go into the whole matter in detail, but our people out there want to see that road a success. They are interested in it. They believe that it could be made a success if there were the proper co-operation between all the people who should be concerned in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this particular matter. This is rather amusing for me, after having been here for eleven sessions and hearing every year this discussion on the Hudson Bay railway and the promises of the minister and the government that they are going to see what can be done about it. It may be new to some of the other members from northern Saskatchewan who are here for the first time, but it certainly is not a new story in this house. In 1946 there was a resolution before the house on which the house voted by an overwhelming majority, asking the government to make greater use of this port.
After hearing this debate, after visiting the port, after living in that part of the province, it seems to me that this government is responsible. Through the harbours board they control the port of Churchill. Through the Hudson Bay railway and the Canadian National Railways they control the railways going to that port, and through the wheat board they control the main product which can be shipped through that port. Therefore they should have some influence on the insurance rates into that port. Therefore the responsibility lies here with this government as to whether that port is to be developed or not. If they see fit it can be developed. If they exhibit the same apathy that they have in the past then the port will remain in the same state as it has been during the last number of years.
With the facilities there the port could handle at least twenty or twenty-five million bushels of grain even during the present season, if it were placed in a position where it could be moved into the port at the proper time. The Hudson Bay railway will only be a paying proposition when this government, through their various government agencies, make up their minds that they are going to develop the port. Through the Canadian National Railways there is the possibility of building feeder lines to Hudson Bay. A new mining area has opened up in the Loon lake

district, north of Flin Flon, where there is a large body of ore which, when developed, could be moved out through Hudson bay. There are several branch lines in northern Saskatchewan. I refer particularly to the one which ends at Arborfield and another which ends at Carrot river which can be connected up with the Hudson Bay railway at Le Pas in Manitoba, and make that railway a paying proposition. In my opinion it is entirely up to this government to decide whether that is done or not, or whether it is going to continue to pay deficits on that road as has been the custom in the past few years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: May I add a voice from Alberta in support of the Hudson Bay railway. I believe the success of that railway is pretty well covered by the old saying that where there's a will there's a way. I hope that before too long the government will acquire a very definite will, and will find a way to make this a success. In western Canada there is a desire that this railway should succeed, and I believe it can be made a success. I ask that it be made so.

Far be it from me to offend the minister because I believe that he believes everything he says. As far as reports are concerned, may I say that I have read a good one that was made in 1906. I made a complete statement n the house on the orders of the day earlier and went into the matter as fully as I could; cut perhaps I can recapitulate briefly. The air agreement which was signed between the ;wo countries in June, 1949, provided among nany other things that T.C.A. would operate ;he route between Montreal and New York. They made their application to the civil leronautics board in the usual course, and Colonial Air Lines by a number of legal nethods, attempted to block the application. Che position is such that it would take some ime to go into the legal entanglements involved in that application.
Be that as it may, T.C.A. have not yet )btained their right from C.A.B. to operate o New York. On the other hand C.A.B. ;ave us the right to have Canadian Pacific \ir Lines operate between Vancouver, Hono-ulu and Australia, and another application s now before the civil aeronautics board by
Supply-Transport
T.C.A. to operate into the Caribbean via Florida with traffic rights at St. Petersburg and Tampa, which as yet has not been disposed of. Because of the delays in the granting of the licence to T.C.A. and because of what appeared to the air transport board to be lack of good faith on the part of Colonial the board under the Aeronautics Act issued this show-cause order, which simply means that Colonial Air Lines will be asked to come before the board and show cause why its licence to operate between New York and Montreal should not be suspended. I do not think I can say more than that at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I do not quite follow the reasoning behind this case. It may be extremely irritating to have Colonial Air Lines opposing the constitutionality of the award of the franchise to T.C.A.; but surely the fact that they have a franchise already to operate from New York to Montreal cannot be disputed. I am inclined to question the wisdom-and I should like to hear the minister's reaction to this

of entering into disputes at the international level concerning a matter which it seems to me should be dealt with at the commercial level. In other words if there is a dispute between two companies, Colonial and T.C.A., why must governments get mixed up in it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Governments are not involved in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then why are we getting notes from the United States government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Governments had not been mixed up in it except to this point, when the note referred to yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was received. The application is simply a routine one made by the air line to C.A B. in the United States and to the air transport board in Canada; there is nothing more than that in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Following the minister's
statement, as I understood his remarks the other day no matter what may be the outcome of Colonial's application, nothing will interfere with the use of Gander by United States or international air lines?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I am unable to substitute my judgment for that of the board. The air transport board is the body that grants the licences. Already they have granted licences to two United States companies at Gander, PanAmerican and Trans-World Air Lines. One application is still pending; and the rights granted those two United States companies at Gander are permanent. The other right will be disposed of.

Supply-Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Has the minister reason to believe that other trans-Canada carriers will not be granted the same rights?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I have none.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Who inspired-and I shall use that word for want of a better-the show-cause order issued to Colonial Air Lines?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The air transport board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Is that not a branch of government, an emanation of the minister's department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Yes, it is, in the same way as the board of transport commissioners is a branch of the department, or the national harbours board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: It seems to me, with respect, that government is getting mixed up with this. I will put it this way. Why could not T.C.A. have issued the show-cause order?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: T.C.A. is the chosen instrument of the government to operate under the international air agreement, just as Colonial Air Lines is the chosen instrument of the United States government to operate from New York to Ottawa. It could not interfere. There must be a regulating body that decides whether an air line shall operate from one point to another or shall cease to operate. That regulating and controlling body is the air transport board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Is the position not this? Whether we resent it or not, Colonial Air Lines made an application and Colonial is- and I think I am correct in this statement- a commercial air line, is it not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Colonial did not make application. Colonial already had its licence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: It opposed the constitutionality of the award of a franchise to T.C.A. from Montreal to New York.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: But it did that as a commercial entity. Unless the T.C.A. take action to request that Colonial's licence be cancelled, it seems to me that the air transport board, which it is stated is an emanation of the government, has turned around to a commercial corporation and, as it were, by way of reprisal, said: You show cause why we should not cancel your licence. That is why I say I regret that government-and it appears that we have taken this step-should get mixed up in what is a commercial matter as between air lines.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The reverse position could equally have been the case. Suppose that Colonial Air Lines had made the application

and had previously been designated by the American government as being the line to operate between Toronto and New York. T.C.A. could then have come before the air transport board and opposed the application. It probably would not have done so, but it could have done so in the same manner as Colonial is opposing and has opposed the application by T.C.A. before the C.A.B.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That is perfectly true. I do not think that alters the situation as I have placed it before the committee, namely that the action to show cause why Colonial Air Lines licence should not be cancelled has been taken in the first instance by an emanation of our government. Is that not a statement of the fact?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No, that is not the fact. The fact is simply this. The two countries signed a bilateral air agreement and one of the designated instruments of one country, namely Colonial, challenges the right of T.C.A. to operate on a certain route; and it challenges that right, as the hon. member has said, on the ground of constitutionality; and while challenging the constitutionality of the bilateral air agreement, it maintains that it has the right on the other hand to operate from New York into Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Under an earlier agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Under the same agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, under the same agreement, confirmed in the earlier agreement. What I mean is that it had these rights under the earlier agreement and now the same rights were confirmed in the agreement of June, 1949, plus other rights. The whole point is that it seeks to challenge the constitutionality of the agreement in the United States and still in Canada it wants the right to say, on the other hand, that the agreement is constitutional and that it should have the right to operate in here. All the air transport board say is: We now ask you to show cause why your rights should nol be suspended.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Is there no way in which thal action taken by the air transport board could have been taken by T.C.A.?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: In order to keep the thing ofl the international level and keep it as between air lines?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
No, for the reason that T.C.A is not a regulating or governing power. There is only one body that has them under the Aeronautics Act, and it is the air transporl board. It is the only board that can cancel oi

grant a licence or ask an applicant or a licensee to show cause why its licence should not be suspended.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Would it not have been possible tor T.C.A. to apply to the air transport board? Would it not have been possible for that action to have originated with T.C.A.?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: It seems to me to be desirable that it could.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Only in regard to its rights across Canada or a trans-border right wherein it would have to apply to both boards; that is, if it had running rights in both countries, therefore it must get a licence from both countries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: In conclusion, as far as I am concerned, I put this thought before the minister as a result of the discussion we have had. In my view it would be desirable to create a situation in which it would be possible for the initial action to be taken by our T.C.A. or our commercial air lines under such a set of circumstances, if only for the object of avoiding the appearance-and it seems to me it has that appearance, based on facts-of government having to take the initial action which means inevitably what we have now, an exchange of international notes, a thing which has not happened under circumstances of this sort, at any rate, for years as between ourselves and the United States. I think it is most regrettable. I feel that, if it is at all possible, some mechanism should be worked out whereby our commercial air lines, T.C.A. or other air lines as the case may be, could take initial action to avoid such a set of circumstances in the future.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: If the Colonial Air Lines withdrew their application in the United States, would this show-cause summons be dropped?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I could not answer that question. That would be up to the board. I could anticipate what the result would be, but I would not presume to say what the board's decision would be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think there is one question about the jurisdiction of the air transport board which should be clarified. It has always been my understanding that the board exercises its discretion in granting a licence, permit, or whatever the certificate is called, and apparently that has been done in this case. Colonial Air Lines have been given a licence. I can quite understand why the board should at a later date issue a show-cause summons to show why that licence should not be cancelled if there were some doubt about the ability to fly, or if the line were not operating
Supply-Transport
safely, or if there were something being done that was wrong with the actual conduct of the operation; but I should like the minister to state whether the air transport board can go further than that and cancel the licence for some reason which has nothing whatever to do with the efficiency of the operation. If the board can do that with one line, then it could do the same with a Canadian line; having issued a licence to a Canadian line, and that licence still not having expired, and the route being flown in an efficient way, satisfactory to the public, the board could issue a show-cause summons and have that licence cancelled for some extraneous reason. Has the board that power? That is the point which worries me. Because it does not like something that a flying company is doing, quite apart from the route that is being flown, has the board the drastic power to cancel the company's licence?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: In the first place, the licence was granted under the old agreement. In the second place, having the power to grant a licence, they must of necessity have the power to suspend or cancel that licence. And as I said the reason why the show-cause order is being given is perfectly valid, namely, that a licensee claims on the one hand that the air agreement under which it is the chosen instrument is invalid, on one side of the line, and on the other side claims the right to continue to operate because the air agreement is valid. Surely that in itself is a good reason why the board should exercise the power which it has under the act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then the board could not take action of this kind in the case of a licence issued for a domestic flight, that is, a flight within Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I think the board has the power to grant licences for domestic flights in Canada, and also to cancel them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: If it issues a licence in Canada for flying in Canada and the Canadian company is giving satisfactory service, could the board issue a show-cause summons and cancel that licence for some reason quite apart from the fact that the route is not being flown in a safe way?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I would not like to answer that question generally but I would say that if an air line were operating in accordance with the regulations, civil aviation, radio and weather, the board would not attempt to interfere with it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly in connection with this item, and direct my attention more to what the item does not cover than to what it covers. This item deals with contributions subject to the approval of the governor in council, to assist municipalities to improve existing airports, the sites of which have been provided by such municipalities. The

Supply-Transport
situation I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee is that of those communities which are not municipalities. In northern British Columbia, and presumably in other parts of Canada, there are a large number of small communities which are not municipalities, but which, of their own volition and with their own work, have provided the existing airports.
Perhaps it would not be proper to call these airports, but they could be described as airstrips on which aircraft can and do land.	These are not airports asking for
assistance by way of range finders and other types of modern equipment. What I have in mind are those communities where the citizens have literally got out with their picks and shovels, perhaps with horses or trucks, and built the airports now in use.
Perhaps in view of the wording of the item it would be difficult to assist them. I would draw the attention of the minister to what has been done in a few of those cases in my district. The most important of these is the Atlin airport, where the north-south runway of the proposed two-way airport has been cleared from end to end by the people there. It was done in 1940, and has been partially maintained by bulldozers since that time.
During the months of June and July of this year there was an average of three planes per day at that point. This airstrip was built entirely through local effort, local money and local labour.
At Telegraph Creek, which perhaps is not so large, we find a similar situation where the airstrip was built by local, voluntary labour. At Dease Lake we find a somewhat similar airstrip. The main expense of the field at this point was borne by Mr. G. L. T. Dalzeil and Robert A. Farrell. Mr. Dalzeil is the present owner of the land on which the field is located, and put up most of the cash. He is the only one who uses the field at the present time, because he is the only person with a small enough plane.
At Tulsequah the situation is slightly different. The airstrip at Tulsequah was built by the Polaris-Taku Mining Company, who now own it. The strip is used by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and other planes that may be going through in that direction. Permission is given to everyone who wishes to use the strip, and no charge is made for its use.
In all these cases I should like to point out that there are involved a class of people who are not usually dependent upon governments, and who do not make a practice of running to governments to have everything done for them. They have done everything

it is humanly possible for them to do, anc have done it of their own volition. I suggesl they are now entitled to some assistance from this department.
Someone may suggest: Why not incorporate and become municipalities? These communities are too small. You cannot incorporate a working municipality out of a community of 220 or 250 people. But, withoul exception, they are communities which have no rail connection, no passenger steamship connection and, so far as three out of foui of them are concerned, no highway connection. To all intents and purposes therefore they are entirely dependent upon air transport
I would ask the minister whether he could make this vote applicable to communities oi that sort. I would be perfectly willing to see the limit brought down to $4,000 or $5,000 as a maximum for airports of this size. Would he consider applications from that type oi community?

speechtext: What are we subsidizing by this item of $240,000? What is the total amount that we have spent in this sort of subsidy since we started doing it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Getting back to this twenty cents per ton, why should not the Steep Rock people pay that additional twenty cents per ton to the Canadian National Railways so that this money would not have to come out of the public treasury as a subsidy?

speechtext: This was done during the war years. This ore was in great demand, and at that time the government came to the conclusion that it would turn over the movement of the ore to the Canadian National Railways and pay it the subsidy, in accordance with the amount of ore that comes out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we understood that policy in wartime, but the war ended in 1945. This is for the fiscal year 1949-50. How much longer are we, in effect, going to subsidize Steep Rock mines by permitting them to pay twenty cents less per ton than it costs the Canadian National Railways to haul the ore?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The Steep Rock mine pays $1.12 and the government pays twenty cents.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: This is private enterprise. The mines should pay the whole thing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I should like to speak briefly, because some of the junior members from British Columbia have already spoken too much. The Abbotsford airport is situated in the constituency of Fraser Valley and is used on an average of 20 days in the year owing to the fact that Vancouver airport is fogbound and all Trans-Canada Air Lines aircraft land there. speechtext:

R.C.A.F. airport, and we pay no rental of any kind to the R.C.A.F.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then this item is not clear, because it refers to the care, operation and maintenance of the Royal Canadian Air Force airfields. When the minister's department is using that airfield, should it not pay a share of the cosit?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Abbotsford is one airport which has not been transferred to the department. This vote covers only R.C.A.F. airports which have been declared surplus and turned over to us for operation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Then you make no provision for a fog-free field in British Columbia?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I say we make no provision for payment at Abbotsford.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: And you make no provision for that purpose?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No, we do not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: What is the position with regard to the use of airfields? speechtext: Are there payments made by C.P.A.?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: And C.P.A. gets that service free of charge from the department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: And all other airlines do, too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: They all get it free of charge?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Are all companies treated the same? I understand that certain veterans or combinations of veterans formed companies to compete in these services; are they given a share of these subsidies?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I cannot understand this large increase in the one year going to one company which apparently has no competition and where there admittedly has been no increase in wages.

The boat was especially built for the service and was called the Kipawo, the name being made up of the first two letters of the three ports served. The boat was taken over by the navy, used in Newfoundland, sold without loss and the proceeds placed in the consolidated revenue fund of Nova Scotia. Continuous representations have been made to the department and the government to renew this service by boards of trade, town councils, individuals and others. That is the only service in all Canada that was discontinued.
I am sure this was not done for economic reasons, because considerable increases are shown in subsidies paid in connection with other services in Quebec, such as the one between Quebec, Natashquan and Harrington where there is an increase from $127,500 to $448,000. Then there is an increase from $60,000 to $88,000 in connection with the service between Pictou, Nova Scotia, Souris, P.E.I., and the Magdalen islands. In addition there is the large increase of $276,000 in connection with the British Columbia services which we have been discussing.
My views and the views of the different communities that were served are on record and the minister knows what they are. I hope some steps are being taken by the department to renew this service because it saves about 150 miles in travelling between these points. There has been a most unjustifiable denial of a service which has been carried on for 50 years and which was a matter of pride to the people on both sides of the Minas Basin.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I had intended to make a statement on the next item, but in view of the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary West it might be advisable to make it at this time.
The committee will recall the statement I made the other evening with respect to cortisone and ACTH, and the circumstances surrounding them, which I felt could be made public at that time. In view of certain conferences which have since taken place here in Ottawa and elsewhere, it is now possible to supplement that statement.
On November 28 I announced that limited supplies of cortisone manufactured in the United States would be made available after January 1 by Merck and Company Limited, Montreal, for research to be undertaken in Canada. Today I can reveal that, as a result of negotiations that have been going on for some time, Connaught Medical Research Laboratories at the university of Toronto are going to undertake immediately to get production of ACTH under way in Canada for investigation and clinical research by Canadian scientists.
The federal government, the Canadian packing industry and the university of Toronto are all co-operating in the project of producing ACTH in Canada. Supplies of ACTH made available in this country will be allocated exclusively for research by a special committee of eminent Canadian medical men named by the president of the national research council. This committee, besides advising on the allocation of ACTH, will approve financial support for research on both ACTH and cortisone to ensure that all available facilities in Canada are fully utilized to speed the research program. The cost, estimated at about three-quarters of a million dollars in the first instance, will be provided for by the federal government through the national health grants and the national research council.
ACTH, like cortisone, seems to hold promise for the treatment of a number of diseases, but since on the basis of present knowledge only exceedingly small quantities of these drugs can be produced, they will be used exclusively for research to determine their

full effects, to discover new or improved methods of production, and to study the possibility of developing related products having similar efEects. Only by limiting these drugs strictly for research purposes now can we hope for progress in finding out how to produce enough for whatever treatment purposes are proved to be of lasting value.
The medical scientists with whom there has been collaboration have urged that persons suffering from arthritis or other disease for which ACTH and cortisone are possible remedies should not neglect the treatment they may presently be taking. As I mentioned in the house a few days ago, with Dr. Cameron, deputy minister of National Health and Welfare, I had an opportunity in New York recently of discussing these drugs with Drs. Hench and Kendall of the Mayo clinic, who are best known among the many scientists who have been associated with their development and use. Both emphasized to us that no responsible prediction could be given as to when adequate quantities of cortisone will be available for treatment purposes. Canadian medical scientists have urged me to state that the same is true for ACTH.
ACTH-known to scientists as the adreno-corticotrophic hormone-is a substance obtained from the tiny pituitary gland located in the centre of the brain of animals. It gives promise of highly important discoveries which may lead to advances in the treatment of a number of diseases. It is, for example, believed to stimulate the body to produce its own cortisone, which has already been found by Drs. Kendall and Hench of the Mayo clinic to produce "encouraging results" in the treatment of certain types of arthritis.
Up to the present, ACTH is being extracted from the pituitary glands of hogs. This gland is about the size of a pea and only a fraction of it contains the hormone. It is estimated that 1,700 hogs produce a pound of glands, and that 400,000 hogs are needed to yield a pound of ACTH.
At present, the entire production of ACTH in the United States is 60 pounds per year, enough for the continuous treatment of only a thousand patients. ACTH can also be obtained from the glands of cattle and sheep, but the yield is not nearly as large as from hogs.
What I am going to say now is said in part with the view of placing on the record the contribution made in this highly important field by our own Canadian scientists-medical men and chemists, particularly steroid chemists.
Since the interest and help of the Canadian packing industry is assured, the maximum
Supply-National Health and Welfare amount of glands will be collected. This entails special arrangements being made, as the glands must be quickly removed from the slaughtered animal, frozen and kept frozen until processed. Dr. R. D. Defries, the director of the Connaught Medical Research Laboratories, is my authority for saying that during the past few months Armour Laboratories in Chicago have been able to forward limited supplies of ACTH to a few centres in Canada for investigation. Although chemists in Canadian laboratories have been interested in this material for some time there has as yet been no production trere of this drug in more than the most minute experimental quantities.
To ensure a continuing supply of ACTH in this country without drawing heavily upon the necessarily restricted supply available for research in the United States, it is planned to use as large a quantity as possible of pituitary glands from Canadian sources. Small quantities will be used at first to develop a method of production in the Connaught Laboratories and the balance will be forwarded to Armour Laboratories in Chicago, who have developed successful processing techniques and will make a supply of ACTH available for use in this country. I am further empowered to state that as soon as production is well established, in keeping with the general policy of this widely known research organization, the product will be made available at the minimum cost.
To assist in financing this undertaking, with the co-operation of the Ontario department of health, a federal grant has been approved from the funds available for public health research under the national health program. An equal amount is being granted by the medical division of the national research council. These grants will be used for developing the process of production.
In the initial stage of making ACTH and cortisone available for research in Canada, an expenditure of as much as three quarters of a million dollars will probably be required during the first year. It is not possible yet to predict the probable cost in succeeding years. The material purchased by these funds will be very limited and sufficient, as I have already emphasized, for research purposes only.
In order to have a supply of ACTH for assay purposes, the food and drug laboratories of the Department of National Health and Welfare have made arrangements with Canada Packers of Hull for enough hog pituitary glands for [DOT] the preparation in Ottawa of very limited quantities of ACTH.
2970	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Health and Welfare The product of this federal laboratory will be tested for potency and stability against preparations of known strength prepared in Chicago and Toronto. It will then be assigned a potency value and retained as a reference standard for the testing of preparations from all manufacturers. This work is being directed by Dr. L. I. Pugsley, chief of the laboratory services in the food and drug division, who in 1933 worked with Dr. J. B. Collip, then professor of biochemistry at McGill university, on some of the first studies made of ACTH. This Ottawa project is the immediate responsibility of W. D. Snair, who has had considerable experience in the preparation and assay of ACTH, having taken his M.Sc. degree in this branch of endocrinology at the university of Toronto.
The development of ACTH and cortisone is an outstanding example of international co-operation in medical research, and of the value of the free interchange of scientific information. It is a notable fact that although the first regular production of both ACTH and cortisone has taken place in the United States, Canadian scientists have been kept fully advised and are co-operating in this undertaking. For several months we have received progress reports from the officers of our department, and also from Canadian scientists who have attended meetings of the committee of the National Academy of Science in Washington that was established to correlate information in this field. We have also established liaison with those who perhaps can be described as mainly responsible for the development of these new drugs.
Early in the 1920's American research scientists demonstrated that the functioning of the adrenal cortex is under the influence of the anterior pituitary, a tiny gland controlling growth and sexual development as well as influencing the functioning of the adrenal and thyroid glands. In 1933 Dr. J. B. Collip, one of our outstanding research men, then at McGill and now dean of medicine at the university of Western Ontario, demonstrated that what had been believed to be a single, simple hormone from the anterior pituitary gland could be broken up into fractions to perform several functions. One of these fractions is ACTH.
In this work Dr. Collip was assisted by Dr. Evelyn Anderson, now in the United States public health service, and Dr. D. L. Thomson, now dean of graduate studies and research at McGill university. The first report of these studies was published in the English medical journal, the Lancet, in


August 1933. Dr. Hans Selye, also working at McGill at this time, who is now head of the institute of experimental medicine and surgery at the university of Montreal, devised a practical method of removing the minute pituitary glands in animals used for experimental purposes.
Three years later, Dr Selye first announced his theory-which is of great interest-about the body's defensive mechanisms against injury and disease and the way in which they involve the pituitary-adrenal linkage.
It was not until several years later that- at about the same time-Dr. C. H. Li and Dr. H. M. Evans of the university of California and Drs. Sayers, White and Long of Yale university, obtained purified ACTH from the anterior pituitary glands of sheep and swine. Dr. Long also worked at McGill university for some years.
In 1947, J. B. Fishman of Yale university developed a method of preparing ACTH which gave yields considerably higher than those obtained by previous workers, and last year Dr. Li's work opened up the possibility of synthesizing ACTH. Also in 1948, Dr. J. S. L. Browne, professor of medicine at McGill university, and his associates carried out studies on the metabolic effects of ACTH on the human system.
As yet it is beyond the powers of scientists to produce these drugs in quantity. Efforts are being made to find better sources or less complicated and time-consuming production methods. Meanwhile, we are ensuring that funds will be available in Canada to further all useful lines of investigation both into the production and the use of these drugs. To do this we must resolutely conserve them exclusively for research purposes as this is the surest guarantee of shortening the time that must elapse-and it might be a very long time-before they can be made available for all that they can benefit.
I have made this statement in collaboration, of course, with the officers of my department, but also in collaboration with some of the men whose names I have mentioned and who have deemed it necessary to state some of the things I have said. I have done so because of the great importance attached to cortisone and ACTH by leading authorities in Canada, and indeed all over the world. The considerable resources of Canadian scientific research are now being mobilized to ensure a worth-while Canadian contribution in a matter so important to humanity.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

Ottawa, December 7, 1949.
My dear Premier:
In a recent letter the premier of Saskatchewan has inquired whether it is proposed to have an agenda under which to deal with the question of constitutional amendment at the conference opening on January 10.
In my original letter of September 14 the purpose of the conference was described as being to devise a generally satisfactory method of making amendments in Canada to the provisions of the constitution which concern both federal and provincial authorities. It was on that basis that the proposal for the conference was made and agreed to. In my last letter of November 7, I referred to the conference more briefly as being simply "to consider a method of amending the constitution of Canada." It had been the feeling of my colleagues and myself that the subject for discussion at the forthcoming conference scarcely admitted of any formal subdivision or reduction to an agenda of procedure in advance. We had felt that each delegation would be making its own preparations for discussion of the problem of procedure in constitutional amendment, and that the question of the best way of discussing it might be settled after we had assembled on January 10. I should appreciate it if you would let me know whether you feel that this is a satisfactory basis on which to leave the arrangements.
Perhaps I might take this opportunity to refer to .another matter which has been considered by my [DOT]colleagues and myself recently. There are many questions of concern to both the provincial and the federal governments in connection with which some discussion would be desirable. Several questions have been proposed for discussion at various times and there may be others which it would be helpful to consider jointly.
If it would meet with the approval of the governments of the provinces, I would propose that a general conference should be held early in the autumn of 1950, possibly in September or October, to discuss general questions of common concern to the provincial and federal governments. The conference would, among other things, carry out the undertaking which has been given to several of the provincial governments which entered into tax agreements with the federal government to hold a general conference at least a year prior to the expiration of the agreements on March 31, 1952. If the suggestion for a conference meets with your approval, and that of the other provincial premiers, views might be exchanged in the next few months as to the matters that should be placed on the agenda, and preparations could then be undertaken. It would, I think, be desirable to have an interval of several months in which to make preparations if fruitful discussion is to result.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent

Ottawa, December 7, 1949 Hon. T. C. Douglas, M.L.A.,
Premier of Saskatchewan,
Regina, Saskatchewan.
My dear Premier:
I have received your letter of November 29 enquiring as to an agenda for the conference which is to open on January 10 to consider the procedure of amending the constitution of Canada.
In my original letter of September 14 the purpose of the conference was described as being to devise a generally satisfactory method of making amendments in Canada to the provisions of the constitution which concern both federal and provincial authorities. It was on that basis that the proposal for the conference was made and agreed to. In my last letter of November 7 I referred to the conference more briefly as being simply "to consider a method of amending the constitution of Canada". It had been the feeling of my colleagues and myself that the subject for discussion at the forthcoming conference scarcely admitted of any formal subdivision or reduction to an agenda of procedure in advance. We had felt that each delegation would be making its own preparations for discussion of the problem of procedure in constitutional amendment, and that the question of the best way of discussing it might be settled after we had assembled on January 10. In view of your enquiry I am, however, writing to all the provincial premiers to ask whether they think it would be satisfactory to leave arrangements on the basis I have indicated or whether an effort should be made to draw up an agenda.
Perhaps I might take this opportunity to refer to another matter which has been considered by my colleagues and myself recently. There are many questions of concern to both the provincial and the federal governments in connection with which some discussion would be desirable. Several questions have been proposed for discussion at various times and there may be others which it would be helpful to consider jointly. If it would meet with the approval of the governments of the provinces, I would propose that a general conference should be held early in the autumn of 1950, possibly in September or October, to discuss general questions of common concern to the provincial and the federal governments. The conference would, among other things, carry out the undertaking to which I referred in my letter of August 18 to hold a general conference at least a year prior to the expiration of the tax agreements on March 31, 1952. If the suggestion for a conference meets with your approval, and that of the other provincial premiers, views might be exchanged in the next few months as to the matters that should be placed on the agenda, and preparations could then be undertaken. It would, I think, be desirable to have an interval of several months in which to make preparations if fruitful discussion is to result.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent
Friday, December 9, 1949
